2026-11-27 Friday 6 stories

What Talent Needs to Know 3 opportunities · 3 challenges
Opportunities
  • A finished video library can now earn on a second platform with no new production, which makes the right to re-license a creator's back catalog worth keeping out of any exclusive platform or network deal. (Rights Ownership)
  • Skydance has taken next year's debt off the table as a reason to cut film and TV spending, and the next date its owners will be measured against is April 4, when $47 billion of investor stock becomes free to sell. (Company Building)
  • A betting app signed Romo within a month of a network dropping him and paid partly in ownership, which adds prediction and betting platforms to the buyers for on-air sports talent who carry an audience. (Company Building)
Challenges & Headwinds
  • Every dollar the networks and streamers add to NFL fees in next year's renegotiation comes out of the same content budgets that pay for scripted and unscripted series, so the size of those renewals may set how much is left for everything else.
  • A filmmaker making a theatrical-scale picture for Netflix still gets a limited booking by default, so the screen count and the length of the theatrical run may need to be written into the deal before production starts.
  • Every major service except Netflix is signing subscribers at $2.99 to $5 a month, which makes how a backend deal defines streaming revenue, list price or what the service actually collects, matter more than the subscriber count.
The NFL Is Taking a Bigger Share of a Shrinking TV Ad Market
NFL games drew $5.87 billion in advertising last season, up 6.8%, while Madison & Wall expects U.S. TV advertising outside political spending to fall 2.4% in 2026.
The NFL spread five games across Thanksgiving week this year, with Netflix and Prime Video joining CBS, Fox and NBC. Guideline projects $6.26 billion in NFL ad revenue this season, and Emarketer puts sports at 31.8% of U.S. TV ad spending. TheWrap reports the league renegotiates its contracts with each media partner in the coming year. Octagon's Dan Cohen said the weakness of other programming is "doing more of the work" in raising the league's value. The piece names the open question: how buyers keep paying NFL fees while still funding scripted and unscripted shows.
Potential Talent Implication: Every dollar the networks and streamers add to NFL fees in next year's renegotiation comes out of the same content budgets that pay for scripted and unscripted series, so the size of those renewals may set how much is left for everything else.
The Facts
  • NFL ad revenue: $5.87B in the 2025-26 season (+6.8%), projected $6.26B this season (Guideline).
  • U.S. TV advertising excluding political: expected -2.4% in 2026 (Madison & Wall).
  • Sports share of U.S. TV ad spend: 31.8% this year (Emarketer).
  • Regular-season NFL ad revenue 2025-26 (Guideline estimates): Fox ~$1.13B; NBC and Peacock ~$996M; CBS ~$902M.
  • Thanksgiving 2026 slate: Netflix Packers-Rams (Wednesday), traditional Thursday tripleheader, Prime Video Broncos-Steelers (Black Friday).
  • Amazon: 80 advertisers new to the NFL since Thursday Night Football began in 2022; TNF advertisers up 6% year over year; interactive ads showed 27% higher purchase rates (Billy Davis, Amazon Ads).
  • Netflix: Peters said six of its 10 biggest sign-up days in five years were tied to live events; Ampere estimated ~430,000 U.S. subscriptions around Christmas 2025 (NFL plus Stranger Things).
  • Peacock: Antenna estimated ~3 million sign-ups around the January 2024 Chiefs-Dolphins playoff exclusive.
  • Streaming was 49.6% of U.S. TV viewing in August vs 17.5% for broadcast (Nielsen); NFL regular season averaged 18.7M viewers in 2025.
  • Quote, Dan Cohen (Octagon Media Rights Consulting): "Both, but the second reason is doing more of the work."
  • Quote, Cohen: "The broadcasters use the NFL to protect reach."

Netflix Kept Fincher's $120 Million Cliff Booth to 252 Theaters Over Thanksgiving
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is tracking a $4.85 million five-day at 252 theaters, about $19,200 per screen, against $7,000 a screen for last year's Wake Up Dead Man at 600.
Deadline estimates the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel took $910,000 on Wednesday in a limited booking helped by AMC's Imax screens. David Fincher told Collider the film cost $120 million to $123 million, not $200 million. Deadline wrote that Netflix is leaving "soooo much money on the table" and could have earned at least $20 million by going wide; the original grossed $142.8 million domestic. Elsewhere, Disney's $200 million original animated Hexed is tracking a $35 million five-day, close to 2023's Wish, while Lionsgate's Sunrise on the Reaping leads at $85 million plus.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A filmmaker making a theatrical-scale picture for Netflix still gets a limited booking by default, so the screen count and the length of the theatrical run may need to be written into the deal before production starts.
The Facts
  • Cliff Booth: 252 locations (251 in the Wednesday update); Wednesday ~$910K; 3-day ~$3.3M; 5-day ~$4.85M; 5-day per-theater ~$19.2K.
  • Comparison: Wake Up Dead Man (Netflix, Thanksgiving 2025) played 600 sites, ~$7K per theater, $4.25M 5-day.
  • Cost per Fincher (to Collider): $120M-$123M.
  • Once Upon a Time in Hollywood domestic: $142.8M.
  • Sunrise on the Reaping (Lionsgate): $15.1M Wednesday, 5-day forecast $85M+, 3-day $58M+ (-51%), running cume ~$233M by Sunday; global openings this year $226.1M (Sunrise) and $218.8M (Michael).
  • Hexed (Disney, $200M production cost): $7.6M Wednesday incl. Tuesday previews; 3-day ~$20M; 5-day ~$35M; A- CinemaScore. Wish (2023): $175M cost, $31.6M 5-day, $63.9M domestic final.
  • Focker In-Law (Universal/Paramount, $90M net): 5-day ~$36M; B+ CinemaScore.
  • Thanksgiving 2025 five-day total: $290.3M; record is $424.9M (2024).
  • Deadline: "Still no word out there whether or not Lionsgate rejected or accepted Legendary's bid."

Spotify Pays Creators for Videos They Already Made for YouTube
Tom Walters, a physical therapy creator with 1.2 million YouTube subscribers, earns $1,000 a month on Spotify from 3,000 followers by re-uploading old videos, against $8,000 a month from YouTube.
Spotify began paying video creators through its Partner Program last year, sharing Premium subscription and ad revenue. Ryan Trahan and Nick DiGiovanni have reached its podcast charts by re-uploading existing videos, and an April fitness hub added creator workout videos. Walters, invited into the program, told The Publish Press he moved his YouTube catalog over unchanged; per follower, Spotify paid him about 50 times what YouTube did. He said revenue rose only when Spotify promoted his videos, because his YouTube views come from search and Spotify users do not search for that content.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A finished video library can now earn on a second platform with no new production, which makes the right to re-license a creator's back catalog worth keeping out of any exclusive platform or network deal.
The Facts
  • Spotify Partner Program has paid video creators since last year; revenue share of Premium subscriptions and ads.
  • Creators on Spotify podcast charts from re-uploads: Ryan Trahan, Nick DiGiovanni.
  • April 2026: Spotify launched a fitness hub with creator workout videos.
  • Tom Walters: 1.2M YouTube subscribers; ~$8K/month YouTube AdSense; ~$1K/month Spotify with ~3K followers; roughly 50x more per follower on Spotify.
  • Quote, Walters: "I literally have just pulled the YouTube videos over."
  • Quote, Walters: "Most of my views on YouTube come from search. That's the culture that's built there."
  • Walters saw no significant lift outside the month Spotify promoted his content.

Skydance Has Paid Off Its 2027 Debt, and $47 Billion in Investor Stock Unlocks April 4
Skydance repaid $3.9 billion on Warner Bros. Discovery's receivables facility and is redeeming about $700 million of 2027 notes, leaving roughly $168 million due next year, its 8-K says.
The filing says Skydance ended the $4 billion WBD securitization facility (borrowing against money customers owe) on November 20 and called three 2027 note series for redemption at par on December 23 and 29. It also registered for resale the roughly 3.9 billion non-voting Class B shares that PIPE investors (private buyers of public stock) paid $47 billion for to fund the WBD acquisition. Those shares stay locked up until April 4, 2027. The Ellison family and RedBird still own all of the Class A voting shares.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): Skydance has taken next year's debt off the table as a reason to cut film and TV spending, and the next date its owners will be measured against is April 4, when $47 billion of investor stock becomes free to sell.
The Facts
  • Filer: Skydance Corporation (NYSE: SKYD), Form 8-K, date of earliest event November 20, 2026; filed November 27, 2026.
  • Item 1.02: WBD Receivables Funding paid off and terminated the $4.0B Receivables Purchase Agreement (PNC Bank administrative agent) on November 20, 2026; ~$3.9B outstanding repaid.
  • Item 8.01 redemptions at 100% of principal: Paramount Global 2.90% Senior Notes due 2027 ($584,271,000, Dec 23); Warner Media 3.80% Notes due 2027 ($33,400,000, Dec 23); Discovery Communications 1.90% Senior Notes due 2027 (EUR 84,285,000, Dec 29).
  • Remaining 2027 maturity after redemptions: ~$168M Discovery Global Holdings 3.755% Notes due March 15, 2027 (not callable at par).
  • PIPE: ~3.9B Class B shares for $47B; lock-up until April 4, 2027; resale registered via prospectus supplement to Form S-3 (File No. 333-297906).
  • Also registered: shares under the August 7, 2025 registration rights agreement (Paramount-Skydance close), no longer locked up.
  • Voting control: Ellison family and RedBird Capital Partners own 100% of Class A voting shares through Harbor Lights Entertainment.
  • Filing language: "registering any shares with the SEC does not mean those shares will necessarily be sold."

Netflix Is the Only Major Streamer Not Discounting for Black Friday
HBO Max cut its ad tier 50 percent for a full year, Fox One cut 75 percent for a month, Starz priced twelve months at $11.99, and Netflix offered no discount, as it never has.
HBO Max charges $5.49 a month for a year on its ad tier; Paramount+ is $2.99 a month for two months while parent Skydance prepares a discounted HBO Max and Paramount+ bundle for early next year. Peacock is $2.99 or $8.99 for three months, Disney+ and Hulu $5 a month for a year, and Apple TV $6.99 for six months against a usual $14.99. The Paramount+, Fox One and Peacock offers run out as the NFL playoffs begin. Netflix, whose stock THR says is half its all-time high, is not discounting.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Every major service except Netflix is signing subscribers at $2.99 to $5 a month, which makes how a backend deal defines streaming revenue, list price or what the service actually collects, matter more than the subscriber count.
The Facts

NetflixNo discount (has never offered one)

Paramount+Premium and standard plans $2.99/month for first two months

PeacockSelect $2.99/month, Premium $8.99/month, first three months
Disney+ and Hulu$5/month for one year
Apple TV$6.99/month for six months (usual $14.99/month)
Starz$11.99 for 12 months on the annual plan

  • The Paramount+, Fox One and Peacock offers are time-limited and end as the NFL playoffs begin; NBC, CBS and Fox hold playoff rights.
  • Disney is expected to sunset the standalone Hulu app; Hulu continues as a service within Disney+.
  • THR: Netflix stock "has been cut in half from its all-time high."

Tony Romo Is Now an Equity Partner in Jake Paul's Betting App
Betr, the betting and predictions app co-founded by Jake Paul and Joey Levy, signed Romo as "chief predictions officer" and equity partner a month after CBS Sports cut ties with him.
Romo, CBS Sports' longtime lead NFL analyst, left the network last month; CBS suspended him after a summer arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated, cut ties months later, and replaced him with JJ Watt. His first media job since is with Betr. THR reports the role is a media play: original content, sports predictions and marketing, starting this week in social video alongside Paul. Levy said Romo "is becoming an equity partner in Betr." No compensation or equity figures were disclosed. THR notes Fox's Greg Olsen is looking for a new TV home.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): A betting app signed Romo within a month of a network dropping him and paid partly in ownership, which adds prediction and betting platforms to the buyers for on-air sports talent who carry an audience.
The Facts
  • Betr: betting and predictions app co-founded by Jake Paul and Joey Levy; describes itself as a "Super App" for gaming and entertainment.
  • Romo's title: "chief predictions officer." Duties: original content, sport predictions, face of the brand in marketing; starts this week in social video with Paul.
  • Levy: "Tony is becoming an equity partner in Betr and will play a meaningful role in how we connect with fans across our Super App."
  • Romo: "Now I get to put those instincts to work in a completely new way with Betr."
  • CBS Sports: suspended Romo after a summer arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated; formally cut ties months later (exit last month); JJ Watt replaced him in the booth.
  • Context in THR: Fox's Greg Olsen looking for a new TV home; networks pursuing Travis Kelce and Sean McVay; Joe Buck and Troy Aikman feud at ESPN.
  • Not disclosed: salary, equity percentage, term.

Three in Four New Microdramas Outside China Are Made With AI, and Few Apps Make Money
Media Partners Asia puts 2026 microdrama revenue at $20 billion, but apps outside China spend 56 cents of each dollar on marketing, and U.S. revenue fell 2% to $1.71 billion.
Media Partners Asia's second annual Micro-Drama Economy report estimates global revenue up 24% to $20 billion, 76% of it in China. Outside China the business is $4.87 billion and thinly profitable: another 18 cents per dollar goes to app stores and payment providers, DramaBox earned a 3.2% net margin in 2025 and ReelShort lost $12 million. New title listings outside China rose from about 100,000 to 440,000, and 75% were made with AI at about a tenth of the cost of a Los Angeles shoot. Live action still leads the top titles on most platforms MPA tracks.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): AI has filled the catalogs but not the top of the charts, where live action still leads, and MPA says the platforms that earn back their marketing will be those with established IP, stars and audiences of their own.
The Facts
  • Global microdrama revenue 2026: $20B, up 24% year on year; forecast $32B by 2031 (9.8% a year).
  • China: $15.2B, 76% of the total, after 90% growth in 2025; ByteDance (Hongguo, Douyin) earns 59% of China revenue; ByteDance, Tencent and Kuaishou together 82%. Advertising is 69% of China revenue in 2026, forecast 79% in 2031.
  • Outside China: $4.87B; forecast $11B in 2031. U.S. is the largest market at $1.71B, down 2% year on year, and will be overtaken by Asia Pacific ex-China by 2029.
  • Cost structure outside China: 56 cents of each revenue dollar to marketing, 18 cents to app stores and payment providers.
  • DramaBox: 3.2% net margin in 2025. ReelShort: $12M loss in 2025, $8M profit in Q1 2026. DramaBox and GoodShort announced a merger at the end of October.
  • DramaBox/GoodShort, ReelShort, Kunlun and NetShort hold 65% of revenue outside China; all are Chinese-owned or backed.
  • India: revenue tripled in 2026 to $322M, the largest Asian market outside China; JioStar launched Tadka on JioHotstar in April.
  • MPA expects TikTok to dominate outside China, "positioned on every side" (selling apps' ads, carrying their series, and competing through its free app PineDrama). YouTube and Meta are not expected to make a major impression.
  • New title listings outside China: about 100,000 in 2025, 440,000 in 2026; 75% made with AI. An AI-made title costs "about a tenth of a series filmed in Los Angeles."
  • Vivek Couto, CEO, MPA: "The leading apps spend more than half of their revenue to acquire viewers, and most of those viewers do not pay."
  • Myat Pan Phyu, lead analyst, MPA: "Viewing has moved far less: live action still dominates the leading titles on most of the platforms we track." And: what decides platform economics "favours companies with established IP, stars and audiences of their own."

Sky Cut Its Film Buying Team, and Universal Is Its Last Exclusive Studio Supplier
Four executives are leaving Sky's acquisitions team, including the buyer of independent UK films, after Sony moved its global pay-1 deal from Sky to Netflix in January.
Comcast-owned Sky has restructured the team that buys pay-TV rights to films (pay-1 is the first pay-TV window after theatrical), a year after cutting its separate Sky Original film unit from seven executives to three. Sky says its strategy is unchanged; UK distributors worry a smaller team will respond more slowly. Sky buys about 40 to 50 films a year from independent UK distributors. Its Paramount and Warner Bros. output deals are non-exclusive and may be renegotiated after the merger, leaving Universal as its only exclusive studio partner.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Independent films that need a UK pay-TV sale to close their financing now face a Sky with a smaller buying team, Sony's films gone to Netflix and its Paramount and Warner Bros. output deals open to renegotiation.
The Facts
  • Leaving: Benedicte Steinsrud, head of acquisitions for Sky Cinema and Sky Store (joined 2024 from Viaplay; relocating for family), plus three others, understood to include the executive sourcing independent features from UK distributors and the executive acquiring independent series.
  • Remaining leadership: Katie Keenan, group director of acquisitions; Lucy Criddle, director of acquisitions and strategic projects. Rachel McCartney's acquisitions manager role becomes film-focused. Facundo Bailez becomes head of acquisitions and editorial; Hadi Leclercq takes a head of commercial role.
  • Sky statement: no change to acquisitions strategy or direction in any genre, including film.
  • Sky Original film team (all rights to 10 to 15 films a year): cut from seven executives to three last year.
  • Independent buying: about 40 to 50 films a year from UK independent distributors; recent buys include William Tell, Pets On A Train (Altitude), The Toxic Avenger, Beast Of War (Signature).
  • Studio supply: Sony agreed a global pay-1 deal with Netflix in January, replacing Sky. Paramount and Warner Bros. deals are non-exclusive and may be renegotiated after their merger. Universal is the only exclusive pay-1 studio partner. Entertainment Film's titles (e.g. Marty Supreme) now go to Amazon for pay-1.
  • Premieres: Sky has moved from a new film every night to three premieres a week on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
  • Context: 1,000 Sky job cuts announced in 2024; original children's commissioning stopped in 2025; Sky's acquisition of ITV expected to close soon.
  • Screen: Sky may try to replace Sony titles with more from Lionsgate and Studiocanal, or with more independent films.

A Judge Stopped the FCC Review of ABC's Licenses and Called It Likely Retaliation
Judge Loren AliKhan blocked the FCC's early review of ABC's eight station licenses, citing ABC's move of a Jimmy Kimmel Live guest segment to YouTube as evidence the review was already chilling speech.
U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan granted ABC a preliminary injunction (a court order that holds until the case is decided) halting the FCC's early renewal review of its owned stations' licenses, finding ABC likely to win its First Amendment retaliation claim and calling it "not a close case." She cited editorial changes ABC had already made, including posting James Talarico's Kimmel appearance on YouTube and livestreaming a Trump primetime speech. She denied a broader order barring other FCC pressure. The FCC called the ruling "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law."
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): The judge stopped the license review but refused to bar other FCC pressure, and ABC has already moved a Jimmy Kimmel guest segment to YouTube, where the agency has no authority, to keep it off broadcast.
The Facts
  • Court: U.S. District Court, Judge Loren AliKhan; preliminary injunction issued Wednesday, November 25, 2026.
  • Holding: the FCC may take no further action in its early license renewal proceeding; ABC is "likely to succeed" on its retaliation claim. "This is not a close case."
  • Scope limit: the judge denied ABC's request for a broader injunction against FCC actions "to coerce or threaten" ABC over content, saying such an order cannot issue against something "merely feared."
  • Jurisdiction: the judge rejected the FCC's argument that the claim belonged in the D.C. Circuit under the Communications Act.
  • Chilling evidence cited: ABC placed James Talarico's Jimmy Kimmel Live appearance on YouTube, outside FCC authority, and livestreamed Trump's July primetime speech out of concern about retaliation.
  • Background: ABC sued in August after the FCC ordered early review of the licenses of its eight owned stations; the first license was not due to expire until 2028. The order came a day after Trump posted that Kimmel should be fired.
  • FCC position: the early review stemmed from ABC not producing documents in a DEI investigation; the judge did not find that explanation credible.
  • ABC News spokesperson: "an important victory for the First Amendment."
  • FCC spokesperson: the granted portion is "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law"; the agency "looks forward to prevailing in full."
  • Commissioner Anna Gomez: the agency has "weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters."

Channel 4 Will Require Producers to Join Britain's Conduct Watchdog, and Netflix Has Not Signed
CIISA's first member register includes Disney, Amazon, Apple TV+, Warner Bros., NBCUniversal and Paramount Skydance; the watchdog has taken more than 90 whistleblowing reports since June.
Britain's Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA, an industry-funded body that takes reports of harassment and bullying) published its member register on November 25 after an event in Parliament. Every UK public service broadcaster, Disney+, Prime Video, Apple TV+, Banijay, Fremantle and Sky signed on; members pay up to 0.1% of UK turnover. Netflix has not joined; a spokesperson said it is "actively exploring working together." Channel 4's Priya Dogra told MPs last week that production companies making its programmes, including news producer ITN, must become members.
Potential Talent Implication: Freelancers on UK productions, the group a select committee chair named as least protected, now have an independent place to report harassment on shows for most major buyers, though not yet on Netflix productions.
The Facts
  • Register published November 25, 2026, following a Parliament event on preventing harmful behaviour in the creative industries.
  • Members include: The Walt Disney Company, Amazon, Banijay, Warner Bros. Entertainment, NBCUniversal, Paramount Skydance, Fremantle, all UK public service broadcasters, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV+, BBC Studios, ITV Plc, Sky TV, House Productions, Element Pictures, the Film Distributors' Association, Film London, British Film Commission, Bafta, the British Independent Film Awards, Edinburgh International Festival and PRS for Music.
  • Funding: voluntary, sliding scale; no member pays more than 0.1% of UK turnover.
  • Reports: whistleblowing open since June 2026; more than 90 reports received.
  • Netflix: not on the register. Spokesperson: "We are supportive of CIISA and we are actively exploring working together." Netflix funded CIISA's development phase and is understood to be in talks.
  • Channel 4: Priya Dogra told a CMSC committee hearing that production companies making programmes for the broadcaster, including ITN, must be CIISA members.
  • Culture secretary Lisa Nandy previously rebuked Banijay for not supporting CIISA.
  • Olivia Bailey, chair of the Women and Equalities Select Committee: harassment is "exacerbated by power imbalances and a lack of protections, particularly for those outside of regular employment structures."
  • Helena Kennedy chairs CIISA; Jen Smith is chief executive.

MS NOW Anchors Backed Their Writers on Pay for Digital Work Made on Top of TV Jobs
Rachel Maddow, Jen Psaki, Chris Hayes and Nicolle Wallace signed a WGAE letter before the December 3 contract expiry; the guild wants 5% raises, and Versant offers a guaranteed 3%.
The Writers Guild of America, East says MS NOW hosts and guests signed a letter backing the roughly 300-member union, which wants inflation-level raises, AI protections and recognition of 50 more staff. The letter objects that Versant Media expects staff "to work extra hours creating new digital content, without treating it as extra work or paying for it." Per the network, the guild seeks 5% a year; MS NOW offers 3%, a higher night-shift allowance and AI protections.
Potential Talent Implication: The dispute turns on whether digital content made on top of a television job counts as paid extra work, and the network's best-known anchors have now put their names behind the writers' answer.
The Facts
  • Union: MS NOW Union (WGAE), about 300 members; first contract reached in 2023 with 3% annual raises; current contract expires December 3, 2026.

Netflix Is Now the Syndication Buyer, and Agents Say It Pays Far Less
Netflix now carries more current ABC, NBC, CBS and Fox series than ever, usually one season after broadcast, and the Mayor of Kingstown producers used Netflix's demand for the show to get a fifth season.
Deadline reports that non-exclusive Netflix licenses, often sold after a show's first season, have replaced off-network syndication, which once required four seasons and 100 episodes. Studios carrying deficits say they look at the money first and now sell to Netflix, Amazon, Roku and Tubi at once. Agents say the proceeds do not come close to syndication for covering deficits and paying profit participants, and are below what Netflix paid for exclusive rights early in the streaming wars. Recent deals include Disney's package with Percy Jackson for a three-month window and AMC's $500 million Walking Dead license.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Backend on a network show now comes from several smaller, non-exclusive streaming licenses instead of one syndication sale, and a show Netflix specifically wants is leverage, as the Mayor of Kingstown producers showed by trading its inclusion for a fifth season.
The Facts
  • Structure: Netflix and other third-party streamers now take network shows out-of-season and non-exclusively; the networks' sibling streamers keep in-season (next day) and prior-season rights.
  • Two entry points: a season lands on the streamer 30 days after its finale (Grey's Anatomy, Sullivan's Crossing), or about 30 days before the next broadcast season (Happy's Place, St. Denis Medical, Doc, Will Trent, Shifting Gears, Best Medicine, Animal Control).
  • Old syndication bar: four seasons and 100 episodes before local and cable sale. Industry veteran: streaming took that window "not after four years, after one year."
  • Studio executive: "we're going to look at the money first, and then the marketing aspect second."
  • Industry insider: "Studios are carrying deficits on these shows, they need to find revenue."
  • Agents (per Deadline): streaming money "doesn't come close to the syndication windfall in covering shows' deficits and paying profit participants"; proceeds are also down from the early streaming-war era of exclusive SVOD deals.
  • TV executive: revenue now comes from Netflix, Amazon, AVOD, Roku and Tubi, and in aggregate rarely reaches peak syndication for one show.
  • Disney-Netflix deal: multi-year Will Trent and Shifting Gears licenses; Percy Jackson and the Olympians for a three-month window; the Ice Age franchise, timed to Ice Age: Boiling Point on February 5, 2027.
  • AMC-Netflix: $500 million license for The Walking Dead universe.
  • Paramount-Netflix (January): 20 series including Paramount+ original Mayor of Kingstown. Deadline hears Netflix would not take the package without Kingstown, and its producers used that to secure a fifth and final season Paramount+ had not planned.
  • Ted Sarandos on licensing: "Our deals bring in much needed revenue. They certainly build awareness, and the benefit of that awareness transfers back to them."
  • From (MGM+, Amazon): first three seasons licensed to Netflix; more than 5 billion U.S. minutes viewed in its first three weeks.

Disney Gave Its New CTO Control of AI Across Every Unit, and Senior Tech Executives Are Leaving
Karandeep Anand, Character.ai's former CEO, joined Disney in September to standardize AI across its units; studio CTO Eddie Drake has since taken early retirement and Jamie Voris has left.
TheWrap, citing two unnamed people, reports that CEO Josh D'Amaro gave Anand broad powers to replace the business units' own production pipelines with standardized AI systems, and that coming layoffs could push the units to comply. A Disney source called that a mischaracterization of its strategy. Disney is targeting $3 billion in annual run-rate savings by fiscal 2029, which D'Amaro says will be reinvested in content and technology. It has signed Adobe to build custom Firefly models trained on Disney IP and puts the AI-generated series Ozzy Fox on Disney+ on December 5.
Potential Talent Implication: Disney is moving AI decisions out of the individual studios and into one central technology office, which may put the people who decide how AI touches a production outside the creative units that talent actually negotiates with.
The Facts
  • Karandeep Anand: former CEO of Character.ai, joined Disney in September as its first chief technology officer; D'Amaro described a "really expansive remit" over infrastructure, data, product, engineering and AI platforms.
  • Mandate (per TheWrap's sources): standardize AI workflows and systems across business units that run their own proprietary pipelines.
  • Departures: Jamie Voris, who ran the Office of Technology Enablement, has left; Eddie Drake, CTO of Walt Disney Studios, took the early retirement program; some lower-level leaders took buyouts.
  • Unnamed source: "He's made a bunch of enemies."
  • Disney source: "the suggestion that workforce reductions are being used to force adoption of a centralized technology or AI solutions is a mischaracterization of our strategy."
  • Cost target: annual run-rate savings of $3 billion by fiscal 2029; TheWrap reports managers were told the company is targeting 20% annual cost savings.
  • D'Amaro on the fiscal Q4 call: "We see AI as a real tailwind for experiences."
  • Adobe deal: custom generative models on the Firefly platform trained on Disney property.
  • Ozzy Fox: AI-generated animated series from Paris-based Animaj, on Disney+ December 5 after a YouTube debut in July.
  • Prior approach under Bob Iger: a softer push that spent tens of millions on the Office of Technology Enablement and an OpenAI Sora deal that was scrapped.
  • Cost context cited by TheWrap: VisionQuest's reported budget of nearly $120 million (Forbes); live-action Moana made for $250 million grossed $323 million.

Britain Has a Working Group on Keeping American Productions From Leaving
The BFI has assembled industry bodies to respond to the proposed 20% U.S. federal production credit, after UK spend on film and high-end TV fell 28% in the year to September 30.
Deadline reports that the British Film Institute formed a working group to study the federal credit's effect and the levers Britain could pull in response, including a richer version of its own 25% credit, which the Labour government has shown little appetite to raise. Culture minister Ian Murray said his team takes the implications "incredibly seriously." UK sources say no production has relocated yet; Mobland, House of the Dragon and Guy Ritchie's Dogfight for Netflix are shooting there in late 2026 and next year. Donald Trump has urged Congress to pass the bipartisan bill.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A U.S. federal credit would put two governments in competition for the same large productions, and filmmakers whose projects could shoot in either country may find location becomes something to negotiate on again.
The Facts
  • BFI working group: formed recently with other industry bodies; covers the U.S. incentive plus the commissioning slowdown, falling budgets, job cuts and competing credits elsewhere.
  • BFI spokeswoman: the group will "identify measures which will ensure the UK remains a world-leading home for domestic and international production."
  • U.S. proposal: a 20% federal film and TV credit; Trump called the bipartisan bill "amazing" and urged lawmakers to pass it, possibly in the current lame-duck session.
  • UK credit: 25%; improving it has been discussed for years without government action.
  • UK spend: film and high-end TV spend fell 28% for the year to September 30 (BFI); 2025 included Avengers: Doomsday, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the Harry Potter series.
  • Ian Murray, culture minister, at the British Screen Forum: his team "takes the implications [of the credit] incredibly seriously"; the outcome "remains to be seen."
  • Aardman's Sean Clarke called the credit a "real issue" for the industry.
  • Productions in the UK in Q4 2026 and 2027: Mobland, House of the Dragon, Guy Ritchie's Dogfight (Netflix).
  • Producer Steven Paul, in Doha, called the U.S. incentive "good for the world."

Critics Are Blaming AI for Cliff Booth's Visuals, and Netflix Will Not Say Whether It Was Used
After critics' screenings of David Fincher's The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, YouTuber and director Patrick Tomasso posted that it shows "blatant and egregious AI use"; Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied it.
The Verge reports that social media reaction to last week's screenings, ahead of the November 25 premiere, accused the Brad Pitt film of generative AI imagery, while some critics said the shots looked like ordinary bad CGI. Netflix bought Ben Affleck's InterPositive, which builds AI models that alter footage shot on set, for about $600 million earlier this year. Fincher told the Los Angeles Times, "I'm not a Luddite, so I don't fear the unknown." Nothing in the reporting confirms AI was used.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Netflix owns the AI tools and is not saying whether they touched the film, while Fincher's name carries the criticism; disclosure of AI use in a finished picture is now a reputational question for the director.

  • Netflix: has neither confirmed nor denied AI use on the film.

Cole Sprouse Says Riverdale Paid Real Money Only After the Season Four Renegotiation
On his brother Dylan's Wildmen podcast, Cole Sprouse said a TV contract is fixed for the first three years and actors make "substantial money" only if the show is picked up for a fourth.

Fincher Wants Actors to Shoot the Master and Give the Close-Ups From a Chair for AI
On The Big Picture podcast, David Fincher described sets where the master is shot 20 to 25 times with surface capture, then actors perform "from the clavicles up" in chairs while AI builds the coverage.
Fincher, promoting The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth amid public accusations that the Netflix film used AI imagery, laid out how he would use the technology. Crews still build the set and do hair, makeup and lighting. Cameras film the master with surface capture (a 3D scan of the actors' performance) running at the same time; the over-shoulders and close-ups are then derived from material the actors record seated after the crew moves to the next stage. Asked whether that way of working appeals to him, Fincher said, "Totally." He has not directly addressed the Cliff Booth criticism.
Potential Talent Implication: An actor on a Fincher set would give most of the close-ups from a chair after the crew leaves, so what the contract says about surface capture and shots derived from it may matter more to that performance than the shooting schedule.

  • Fincher: "you hire all the same people... you shoot the master 20, 25 times till you get worked out exactly."
  • Fincher: "You're doing surface capture at the exact same time that you're filming, and then you go in, you set all the actors in chairs wherever they land, and they perform from the clavicles up."
  • Fincher: "All of the iteration, the over-shoulders, the close-ups, all that stuff is derived from the material that you do sitting in a chair after everyone leaves."
  • Fincher: "I won't miss focus in AI and I will land the dolly shot in AI"; "people will only have to do it 15 times."

Brand Deals Now Bar Creators From Using AI in Campaign Content
Pearpop's VP of talent Kurt Stadelman said more brand contracts bar creators from using generative AI in campaign content, and he tells creators to cap paid ad usage at three to six months.
Speaking with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde at Digiday's Creator Strategies event, Stadelman said brands are writing explicit no-AI clauses into influencer deals, and creators are welcoming them. Pearpop has had to clarify the language several times so creators can still use AI in the background for concepts, scripts and performance analysis. Brands also increasingly run creator posts as their own paid ads through whitelisting (running a creator's post from the brand's ad account), so paid usage rights must be written into the deal. His advice: start at three months, never more than six upfront, never perpetuity.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): A creator's brand deal now sells two things in writing, that the content is made without AI and how long the brand may run it as an ad, and the second decides whether the creator can take the next deal in that category.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Kurt Stadelman, VP of talent, Pearpop; in conversation with Sara Jerde, Digiday managing editor, at Digiday's Creator Strategies event (as reported by Parasocial).
  • Stadelman: "We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns."
  • Carve-out Pearpop negotiates: creator may use AI tools in the background (concept, script, performance analysis). "We've had to specify that a few times just to make sure."
  • Paid usage: brands increasingly whitelist creator posts as paid ad units; usage rights must be explicit.
  • Usage advice: three months as a starting point with an option to extend; no more than six months upfront. "Usage in perpetuity should never be agreed to. That's a dangerous place to be for a creator." Perpetual rights block future deals in the same category.
  • Payment: Pearpop pushes for net-30 or net-60 over net-90; brands increasingly miss the payment terms they wrote.

The Academy Ruled the First Fully AI Feature Is Not an Animated Film
"Gods Don't Give Gifts", made entirely with generative AI by a team of 30 to 35 people using human voice actors, was left off the Academy's list of 38 eligible animated features on November 23.
The Academy's Animation Branch Executive Committee found that "Gods Don't Give Gifts", directed by Zack London (Gossip Goblin) with Fable Studios, does not meet its definition of an animated film, which requires movement created "by any human means." Producer Edward Saatchi says they will appeal, citing Richard Linklater's Apollo 10 1/2, which won eligibility on appeal. The film also entered Director, Adapted Screenplay, Visual Effects and Sound, and opens an Oscar-qualifying run on December 4. This year's rules already limit acting categories to credited roles performed by humans with consent and require human-authored screenplays.
Potential Talent Implication: Voice actors and a human-written script were not enough for the animation branch, which judged who created the movement on screen, so on a fully generated film the awards case may rest on the categories where a person's work can be shown, such as screenplay.
The Facts
  • Film: Gods Don't Give Gifts, director Zack London (YouTube name Gossip Goblin), producer Edward Saatchi, Fable Studios. Described by IndieWire as the first fully AI movie released theatrically.
  • Ruling: not on the Academy's list of 38 eligible animated features, announced Monday, November 23. The Animation Branch Executive Committee found it did not meet the definition of an animated film under the rules for the 99th Awards.
  • Rule quoted: an animated film is one in which characters or objects are given the illusion of life "by having movement created for them, by any human means"; at least 75 percent of running time must be animation; running time over 40 minutes.
  • Appeal: Saatchi and London plan to appeal, citing Apollo 10 1/2, originally ruled ineligible and reversed on appeal.
  • Other submissions: Best Director, Adapted Screenplay, Visual Effects, Sound.
  • Production: script by London; characters visually generated with AI; human actors voice the characters; cameos including Grimes; a human team of 30 to 35 worked on it for years.
  • Academy rules this year: acting categories limited to credited roles demonstrably performed by humans with their consent; screenplays must be human-authored; AI use must be disclosed.
  • Hybrid comparison: Coyote vs. Acme, animated and live-action, qualified.
  • Release: Oscar-qualifying run from December 4; expansion January 22 with international distributor AGC International.
  • Quote, Saatchi: "Is it time to consider a 'Best AI Movie?' Do these films fit best in the voice-actor led animation category? Is AI simply the new VFX?"

Goldman Sachs-led lenders pulled Radford Studio Center from Tuesday's auction and sold it to Netflix directly for $380 million, about a fifth of the $1.85 billion Hackman Capital paid in 2021.
Netflix bought the 55-acre Radford Studio Center in Studio City for $380 million on November 24 and, according to Deadline, also paid the city's transfer tax on the sale.   • Prior price: Hackman Capital bought the lot from ViacomCBS for $1.85 billion in 2021 and did not finish its planned upgrades before losing it to creditors.
  • Property: 55 acres, opened 1928; 22 stages, 210,000 sq ft of office space, 172,737 sq ft of support space.

Tidal Will Remove Every Wholly AI Track From December 9
Tidal says 43 percent of tracks delivered in the last 90 days were wholly AI-generated, over 60 percent on November 6, and it already pulls them from the royalty pool.
Tidal, the music streamer once controlled by Block, announced on X that from December 9 it will reject and remove any wholly AI-generated track it detects. It already labels such tracks and removes them from the royalty pool (the money divided among artists by share of streams). About 27 million tracks, roughly 6 percent of its catalog, are tagged as AI, and 96 percent of them had zero streams in the last 90 days. Tidal said it has also taken down more than 65,000 tracks flagged for impersonating real artists.
Potential Talent Implication: Tidal had already cut wholly AI tracks out of its royalty pool before banning them, so on that platform the human artists' share of the pool is protected by policy, and what counts as "wholly" AI is the line that decides who gets paid.
The Facts
  • Policy: from December 9, any wholly AI track detected on Tidal will be "rejected and removed" (Tidal post on X).
  • Current practice: AI tracks already labeled and excluded from the royalty pool.
  • Deliveries: 43% of all tracks delivered in the past 90 days detected as wholly AI-generated; on November 6, over 60% of deliveries.
  • Catalog: about 27 million tracks, about 6% of the catalog, tagged as AI; 96% of those had zero streams over the past 90 days.
  • Impersonation: over 65,000 tracks taken down for suspected artist-name impersonation.
  • Quote, Tidal: wholly AI music intended to impersonate artists "diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans."
  • Ownership note (Deadline): Tidal was formerly artist-backed and once controlled by Jack Dorsey's Block.

A24 Builds Its Slate to Return 1.35 Times on $25 Million to $40 Million Films, Boehly Says
Todd Boehly, who put $19 million of seed money into A24 in 2012, said nine of every 15 A24 films target 1.35 times their money and recover about 0.8 times quickly through windows.
At the Doha Film Festival's industry days, Eldridge founder Todd Boehly described how A24 cofounder Daniel Katz builds a slate. Of 15 films, nine are core titles budgeted at $25 million to $40 million with an expected return of 1.35 times; about 0.8 times comes back quickly, leaving 0.2 at risk. Three are bigger swings that could support more than one film, run at a 1.2 times target. Three go to young directors. Boehly said Katz wants directors and actors coming back so the business is recurring. A24 was last valued at $3.5 billion in June 2024.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A24 accepts a lower return on the three films it thinks can become more than one movie, so a filmmaker with material that could carry sequels is pitching into the part of the slate where Boehly says A24 takes less.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Todd Boehly, Eldridge (about $75 billion in assets, stakes in A24 and Fulwell Entertainment), at the Qatar Film Committee's Doha Industry Days, fireside chat "Playing to Win."
  • Seed money: Boehly provided $19 million when Katz launched A24 in 2012 with David Fenkel and John Hodges. Last public valuation: $3.5 billion, June 2024.
  • Slate model per Boehly, portfolio of 15 films:
- 9 core films: budgets $25 million to $40 million; expected return 1.35 times; about 0.8 times recovered "right away or very quickly," leaving 0.2 times at risk.
- 3 big swings with "the capacity to become multiple films": expected return 1.2 times, accepted for "more enterprise value or longevity."
- 3 films by up-and-coming young directors, requiring time and effort more than capital.
  • Recovery method: Boehly said Katz "was really good at figuring out how am I going to get my money back using different windows."
  • Spring Breakers: cost "a couple million bucks to buy," made "10 million bucks or so very quickly," per Boehly; grossed $31 million.
  • Repeat talent: "He wants the directors coming back… he wants the actors coming back… because then it's not a transaction, it becomes a recurring business with enterprise."
  • Katz background: Guggenheim Partners film finance group, on Boehly's trading floor roughly 2008 to 2012; flagged Stark Investments' Poseidon slate as a likely loss.

In a New York Times essay Saturday, the CAA chief asked the full Congress to pass the No Fakes Act, which the Senate Judiciary Committee approved unanimously in June, before the end of the year.
Bryan Lourd, chief executive and co-chairman of CAA, wrote in a New York Times guest essay published Nov. 21 that the House and Senate should pass the No Fakes Act and send it to President Trump. The bill would create a federal prohibition on nonconsensual digital replicas of any person's voice or likeness and replace state laws with one standard. Lourd said the bill applies "control, consent and compensation" and is backed by SAG-AFTRA, the Motion Picture Association, IBM, Google and OpenAI. He wrote that some artists already license AI likenesses with their consent.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): If the bill passes, consent and payment become the federal floor for any digital replica of a performer, and the AI likeness licenses some artists are already signing would be negotiated against one national standard.
The Facts

  • Status: the No Fakes Act passed the Senate Judiciary Committee unanimously in June; Lourd says there is momentum to pass the full Congress before year end and calls it "one of the few A.I. bills with true bipartisan support."
  • What the bill does (per Lourd): a federal prohibition on creating nonconsensual digital replicas of any person's voice or likeness, famous or not; a uniform federal standard replacing state laws.

Most SAG-AFTRA Members Do Not Earn Enough to Qualify for the Union Health Plan
President Sean Astin said a substantial majority of members miss the $28,090 earnings or 108-day work threshold, and the board voted Friday to form a task force pushing universal health care.
SAG-AFTRA's national board voted unanimously Friday to create a President's Healthcare Task Force to advocate for universal health care, The Hollywood Reporter reports. Astin said the health plan is financially sound but most members do not qualify, because they earn under $28,090 or work fewer than 108 days a year. Under terms negotiated with studios and streamers this year, eligibility premiums and the earnings threshold rise slightly in 2027, with more increases after. Since Nov. 1 the union has again terminated members behind on dues, and thousands have been dropped, according to Variety.
Potential Talent Implication: Health coverage for most working actors depends on reaching $28,090 or 108 days in a slow production year, and the threshold rises in 2027, so a single booking can decide whether an actor is insured.
The Facts
  • Board action (Friday, Nov. 20): unanimous vote to create the President's Healthcare Task Force, a public-policy group to advocate for universal health care.
  • Eligibility: $28,090 minimum annual earnings or 108 applicable days of work per year.
  • Astin: the SAG-AFTRA Health Plan is on strong financial footing, but a substantial majority of members do not qualify.
  • 2027: eligibility premiums and the earnings threshold rise slightly under this year's contract with studios and streamers, with further increases in later years.
  • Dues: as of Nov. 1 the union resumed terminating memberships of members who owe dues; thousands dropped (Variety, via THR).
  • Pressure: Cheyenne Jackson's "One Job Away" campaign (late October) on actors one or a few jobs short of coverage.
  • Union leadership: board extended Duncan Crabtree-Ireland's contract to 2032 on Oct. 24, reportedly with a 15 percent raise; prior published gross salary $1,068,535.

Newsmax Is Suing to Undo Fox's $22 Billion Roku Deal Two Weeks After It Closed
Newsmax says Fox's Tubi and The Roku Channel together hold about 71% of U.S. viewing time in free ad-supported streaming, enough to limit rival networks' reach.
Newsmax filed a federal antitrust suit in California on Wednesday seeking to unwind Fox Corp.'s $22 billion acquisition of Roku, which closed Nov. 6 after the Justice Department ended its review, TheWrap reports. Newsmax distributes its Newsmax2 channel through The Roku Channel and says Fox could make it harder for rival networks to get favorable placement. Fox had committed to keep Roku open to competing content and not to disadvantage rival services in search results, and called the complaint wholly without merit.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): By Newsmax's count about 71% of free streaming viewing now sits on two Fox-owned services, so anyone selling a free ad-supported channel negotiates placement and search position with a company that owns competing channels.
The Facts
  • Plaintiff: Newsmax; federal antitrust suit filed Nov. 18, 2026, in California federal court.
  • Target: Fox Corp.'s $22 billion acquisition of Roku, completed Nov. 6, 2026.
  • DOJ closed its investigation Nov. 6, finding competition from other streaming providers made substantial harm unlikely.
  • Fox commitments: keep Roku open to competing content; not disadvantage rival services in search results.
  • Newsmax claim: Tubi plus The Roku Channel account for about 71% of U.S. viewing time in free ad-supported streaming (FAST).
  • Chris Ruddy, Newsmax CEO: "This merger represents an extraordinary threat to competition, consumer choice, and the ability of independent news organizations to reach the American public."
  • Fox: "Newsmax's complaint, which comes after a rigorous review process by regulatory agencies, is wholly without merit."
  • Separate earlier Newsmax suit against Fox over cable-news dominance remains unresolved.

  • Until Rice names a film chief, a filmmaker pitching a Netflix movie is pitching him directly, and his last job, at A24, was shepherding auteur projects like Alex Garland's Elden Ring.
  • Burial Hill is close to recovering roughly half or more of its $60 million to $70 million budget from one international pre-sale before cameras roll, with North America still open to a separate buyer. (Project Economics)
  • Sabalenka had a Netflix path and took YouTube because she controls the story and the timing there, and YouTube is now staging premieres to bring brand money to shows the talent owns. (Rights Ownership)
  • Take-Two will only adapt Grand Theft Auto if its own creative teams want it, so any deal for the most valuable unadapted game in the business would start with Rockstar's developers. (Rights Ownership)
  • With rights quoted above $100 million and episodes at $15 million to $25 million, streamers have few slots at that level, and writers and showrunners compete for them on whether the game company trusts them with its players. (Rights Ownership)
  • A24 is staffing 30 to 40 shows largely with first-time creators and showrunners and selling to any streamer, which makes it a buyer of new TV voices while the Warner-Paramount merger cuts the number of other buyers. (New Revenue Stream)
  • Shakman turned a Marvel run into a company of his own with a Disney first look and a staffed development team, and his projects already sit at A24, Paramount+, Mattel and Fifth Season as well as Disney's labels. (Company Building)
  • El Arbi and Fallah now own part of the company that launched them, a business with about 200 million euros in revenue, and they still direct independently. (Company Building)
  • Obsession and Backrooms became Focus's and A24's highest-grossing films on budgets of $750,000 and $10 million, and on a horror film at that cost the backend definition may carry far more of a filmmaker's earnings than the upfront fee. (Project Economics)
  • Pratt now brings Paramount the projects he wants to make and himself as the star on the ones he picks, while his producing work continues at Amazon on The Terminal List and at Apple on Way of the Warrior Kid. (Company Building)
  • Ellison is promising the most content spending of any peer while cutting $6 billion and paying down about $80 billion of net debt, and the 30-film minimum in the states settlement sets the floor on how far film volume can fall.
Challenges & Headwinds
  • Producers and showrunners with deals at either studio now face one buyer where there were two, with the same executives deciding pickups and renewals for HBO Max, Paramount+ and the outside sales business.
  • Selling a Cannes-caliber film to Netflix still costs the filmmaker a shot at the Palme d'Or, because Netflix will not hold the film off French streaming for 15 months.
  • Producers selling into SkyShowtime's European markets lose a regional buyer at the end of 2027, and the reporting does not say which service will carry the Universal and Paramount titles it now holds.
Netflix's New Content Chief Is Running Film Himself Instead of Hiring a Film Boss
Peter Rice has told Netflix staff he will not hire a film chief for now after Dan Lin's exit, and rival executives expect more Netflix films to get theatrical runs within a year.
Peter Rice, Netflix's chief content officer since October, has told staff he is not hiring a replacement for departed film head Dan Lin for now and wants to be in the creative work himself, The Hollywood Reporter reports from multiple sources. Rice built general entertainment at Fox and Disney and most recently had a film and TV deal at A24, where his slate included Alex Garland's Elden Ring. Ted Sarandos says the strategy is not changing but wants bigger U.S. hits, and rival film executives expect more Netflix films to carry a theatrical run a year from now.
Potential Talent Implication: Until Rice names a film chief, a filmmaker pitching a Netflix movie is pitching him directly, and his last job, at A24, was shepherding auteur projects like Alex Garland's Elden Ring.
The Facts
  • Peter Rice became Netflix chief content officer in October 2026, after Bela Bajaria's exit and company layoffs; Dan Lin later left as head of film.
  • Rice is "telling staff that he isn't hiring a film boss for now. He wants to be in the trenches creatively, multiple sources say."
  • Rumors had named ousted Warner Bros. film co-chiefs Pam Abdy and Mike De Luca as possible successors to Lin.
  • Rice's A24 pact credits: Warfare (Alex Garland producing), Chris Rock's Misty Green; development slate included Garland's Elden Ring, A24's biggest production.
  • Ted Sarandos, Oct. 20: "The business and the business flywheel are working. There's no need for a fundamental shift in strategy."
  • Wolfe Research (Peter Supino, Oct. 20): 2026 programming expense grew 10% while U.S. engagement per subscriber "roughly stagnated."
  • Rival film executives believe many more Netflix movies will have a theatrical component a year from now.
  • Theatrical tests named: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (Nov. 25), Narnia: The Magician's Nephew (Feb. 12).
  • Netflix now runs teasers for its own shows before other Netflix programming and launched a brand campaign in theaters and on connected TV, YouTube and TikTok.
  • Reed Hastings (Masters of Scale, late October): the strategy is "more and better television shows, more and better movies."
  • Corroboration (Variety, Nov. 17): La Bola Negra is in a 46-day theatrical rollout, Netflix's longest; Narnia and Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory get exclusive theatrical runs in 2027.

Amazon Is Paying $35 Million to $40 Million for Overseas Rights to an Original Vin Diesel Action Film
Amazon MGM is finalizing an all-rights deal for most territories outside North America on Burial Hill, a $60 million to $70 million film, while North American rights are still in talks.
Vin Diesel will star in Burial Hill, an original action film written by Mike McGrale (Caine) and directed by Jamie Payne (Luther), Deadline reports. Amazon MGM Studios is finalizing a deal for most international rights, excluding a few territories such as CIS, at around $35 million to $40 million, after studio interest kept the project out of the American Film Market. The producers have more funding in place toward a $60 million to $70 million budget. CAA Media Finance arranged financing and handles domestic rights. Deadline compares the move to Amazon's pre-buy of A24's Elden Ring.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Burial Hill is close to recovering roughly half or more of its $60 million to $70 million budget from one international pre-sale before cameras roll, with North America still open to a separate buyer.
The Facts
  • Project: Burial Hill, original action film; Diesel plays a reclusive cemetery groundskeeper; intended to start a franchise.

  • Amazon MGM Studios: finalizing most international rights, all-rights in those territories, "around the $35M-$40M mark"; a few territories such as CIS excluded.

  • Diesel is in production on Fast Forever (2028, Universal).

Warner Bros. Television and Paramount Television Will Become One Studio With More Than 120 Series
Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell will co-run the combined Warner Bros. Television Studios from early 2027, reporting to George Cheeks, whose memo says HR will share more as plans are finalized.
Skydance will fold Paramount Television Studios into Warner Bros. Television Group in early 2027 under the name Warner Bros. Television Studios, Deadline reports. Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell become co-presidents reporting to George Cheeks; CBS Studios, run by David Stapf, stays separate. The combined studio holds more than 120 active series, including The Pitt, Ted Lasso, Reacher, Landman and Emily in Paris. Both studios supplied HBO Max and Paramount+ and sold to outside streamers. Deadline calls cuts inevitable, and BET Studios moves into the new studio.
Potential Talent Implication: Producers and showrunners with deals at either studio now face one buyer where there were two, with the same executives deciding pickups and renewals for HBO Max, Paramount+ and the outside sales business.
The Facts
  • Combined entity: Warner Bros. Television Studios, operating from early 2027; until then both studios operate independently (Cheeks memo).
  • Leadership: Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell, Presidents, reporting to George Cheeks, Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer of Skydance TV. Dungey also chairs Skydance Global Cable Media (50-plus cable brands).
  • CBS Studios (David Stapf) remains the second studio; Skydance Sports Entertainment moves under CBS Studios.
  • BET Studios moves from CBS Studios to Warner Bros. Television Studios.
  • More than 120 active series, including Harry Potter and The Philosopher's Stone (HBO), The Pitt (HBO Max), Ted Lasso (Apple TV), Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage (CBS), Reacher (Prime Video), Marshals (CBS), Landman (Paramount+), Emily in Paris (Netflix), Neuromancer (Apple TV).
  • Layoffs: not announced; Cheeks memo: "HR will share more information as plans are finalized." Deadline: cuts are "inevitable when divisions are merged."
  • Timing: one month after the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger into Skydance closed; 15 months after Paramount Television Studios was relaunched.
  • Cheeks: "Bringing together two of the industry's most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine."

Take-Two Has Not Ruled Out a Grand Theft Auto Film After $1.5 Billion in Presales
Strauss Zelnick said Take-Two would make a Grand Theft Auto film or show only if its own creative teams want to; the series has never been adapted, and GTA VI releases Nov. 19.
Grand Theft Auto VI, the most expensive game ever developed, has an estimated $1.5 billion in presales ahead of its Nov. 19 release, Deadline reports, nearly double the $800 million Grand Theft Auto V took in 2013. Asked on The David Rubenstein Show about film or TV, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said the company would adapt only if its creative teams were passionate about it: "we don't rule it out, but we're very, very selective." Puck's Julia Alexander reports Grand Theft Auto videos have passed 900 billion views on YouTube.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Take-Two will only adapt Grand Theft Auto if its own creative teams want it, so any deal for the most valuable unadapted game in the business would start with Rockstar's developers.
The Facts
  • GTA VI: estimated $1.5 billion in presales; GTA V took $800 million in 2013; 13 years between releases.
  • Release: Nov. 19, 2026 (Deadline, "tomorrow" on Nov. 18). Metacritic score ties The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for highest of all time (Deadline); Variety reports 99.
  • Strauss Zelnick (Take-Two CEO), The David Rubenstein Show: "We would make a movie or television show based on our intellectual property if our creative teams were passionate about it... So we don't rule it out, but we're very, very selective."

  • Comparable adaptations cited: The Witcher (Netflix), The Last of Us (HBO), Super Mario Bros., Sonic, Minecraft; Elden Ring shopped at AFM.

France's 15-Month Streaming Wait Still Keeps Netflix Out of the Cannes Competition
Cannes head Thierry Frémaux wants Joel Coen's Jack of Spades for May 2027, but a competition slot would force a French theatrical release and hold the film off Netflix in France for 15 months.
Netflix is eyeing its first Cannes premiere since 2017 with Joel Coen's Jack of Spades, which it recently acquired, Variety reports from unnamed sources. Competition films must open in French theaters, which triggers France's windowing rules (the required wait before streaming) and would keep the film off Netflix in France for 15 months. Netflix will not accept that, and Ted Sarandos has treated an out-of-competition slot as a deal-breaker. New content chief Peter Rice has known festival head Thierry Frémaux since his Searchlight days.
Potential Talent Implication: Selling a Cannes-caliber film to Netflix still costs the filmmaker a shot at the Palme d'Or, because Netflix will not hold the film off French streaming for 15 months.
The Facts
  • Film: Jack of Spades, directed by Joel Coen; cast Josh O'Connor, Patsy Ferran, Frances McDormand, Lesley Manville, Damian Lewis; now on track for May 2027.
  • Netflix recently acquired the film; Netflix declined to comment.
  • Netflix last premiered films at Cannes in 2017 (Okja, The Meyerowitz Stories); Cannes then required competition films to get a French theatrical release.
  • French windowing: a theatrical release delays French streaming availability by 15 months.
  • Out of competition is the only route; sources say Sarandos has treated that as a deal-breaker.
  • Frémaux has pushed for the film for more than a year; cited Killers of the Flower Moon and Mission: Impossible, The Final Reckoning as out-of-competition precedents.
  • Sarandos earlier told Variety he hoped to "do something special" for Cannes' 80th edition.
  • Netflix bought Emilia Pérez (2024) and La Bola Negra (2026) at Cannes.
  • La Bola Negra is in a 46-day theatrical rollout, Netflix's longest.

Comcast and Skydance Will Shut SkyShowtime, Their European Streamer, at the End of 2027
The board told staff Wednesday that global platforms left regional services short of scale; CEO Monty Sarhan exits and Mark Neil runs the wind-down as interim general manager.
SkyShowtime, the streaming joint venture Comcast and the former ViacomCBS launched in 2021 in more than 20 countries, will wind down in late 2027, The Hollywood Reporter reports from a board memo to staff. The memo says the expansion of major global platforms made it "increasingly challenging for regional players" to reach the scale needed. The service carried Universal, Paramount, Peacock, Sky Studios and Showtime programming. Skydance now counts 203 million HBO Max and Paramount+ subscribers worldwide, and Comcast is spinning off NBCUniversal and Sky next year.
Potential Talent Implication: Producers selling into SkyShowtime's European markets lose a regional buyer at the end of 2027, and the reporting does not say which service will carry the Universal and Paramount titles it now holds.
The Facts
  • Decision: shareholders concluded a strategic review (opened September) and will wind down SkyShowtime in late 2027; service operates normally until then.
  • Leadership: CEO Monty Sarhan exits; Mark Neil is Interim General Manager for the wind-down.
  • Footprint: more than 20 countries; launched 2021 with 10,000-plus hours from Showtime, Nickelodeon, Paramount Pictures, Paramount+ Originals, Sky Studios, Universal Pictures and Peacock.
  • Scale: Sarhan told staff in September the service had "several million subscribers."
  • Skydance: 203 million global subscribers across HBO Max and Paramount+.
  • Comcast: NBCUniversal and Sky spin-off set to close next year.
  • Board memo: "These competitive dynamics have made it increasingly challenging for regional players like SkyShowtime to achieve the scale needed for long-term success."

The Wachowskis Have Served Notice to Take Back The Matrix From Warner Bros.
Lana and Lilly Wachowski formally notified Warner Bros. they are terminating its grant of The Matrix rights, effective as soon as February 2029, while Drew Goddard develops Matrix 5.
Puck's Eriq Gardner reports the Wachowskis served Warner Bros., now part of Skydance, a copyright termination notice (an author's statutory right to reclaim a rights grant after a waiting period). To keep making sequels past that date, Skydance would need a fresh grant. The studio could argue The Matrix was work made for hire, which cannot be terminated, though Warner Bros. said in an earlier lawsuit that the sisters wrote it before their 1994 deal. A Fifth Circuit ruling the Supreme Court let stand this summer allows termination to reach worldwide rights.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A writer who created a franchise before the studio deal now holds a date the owner has to buy past, and under the Fifth Circuit ruling the price could cover worldwide rights, not only the United States.
The Facts
  • Notice: Lana and Lilly Wachowski have formally notified Warner Bros. they are exercising copyright termination rights on The Matrix (Puck, "I've learned"; no named source).
  • Effective date: as soon as February 2029, in the U.S. "and maybe beyond."
  • Matrix 5 is in development with Drew Goddard shepherding; per Puck the sisters have encouraged it and recently increased their involvement. Lilly Wachowski said in September she does not want to "play in that sandbox anymore."
  • Origin: The Matrix was part of a three-picture deal folded together in 1994 (Assassins, Bound, The Matrix). In an earlier copyright lawsuit Warner Bros. appeared to contend the Wachowskis began The Matrix in 1992 and had drafted scripts for all three films by 1993.
  • Precedents (Puck): Skydance negotiated a new deal last year for The Godfather after Mario Puzo's estate exercised termination against Paramount; Annapurna bought The Terminator in 2011 knowing U.S. rights reverted in 2019, and Skydance later dealt with James Cameron.
  • Other terminations Skydance faces (Puck): The Shawshank Redemption, Beavis and Butt-Head, ER (Sherri Crichton, widow of Michael Crichton, is already contesting The Pitt on contract grounds).
  • Law: in BMG v. Vetter the Fifth Circuit held termination can reclaim rights worldwide; the Supreme Court lacked a quorum after four recusals and affirmed by default this summer.
  • Paramount's amicus brief (Lisa Blatt, Williams & Connolly) said worldwide termination would "encourage authors to seek extortionate prices from studios by threatening to sell all rights to make derivative works worldwide to the highest bidder," and called it an "existential threat to the practice of creating derivative works."
  • Disclosure (Puck): RedBird Capital, a Skydance investor, also invests in Puck.

David Ayer Is Now a Partner in an AI Stage Company That Replaces Location Shoots
Ayer joined Ryan Kavanaugh's ACME AI as principal and managing partner; its Grey Box stage puts actors in AI-built locations, and ACME claims 50 to 75 percent savings in time and money.
Director David Ayer (The Beekeeper, Beast) joined ACME AI as a principal and managing partner involved in operations, THR reports. The company, founded by former Relativity Media co-founder Ryan Kavanaugh, runs Grey Box, a performance-transfer stage (actors perform on a soundstage while AI recreates the location around them) that ACME will rent to studios from a dedicated Los Angeles stage. Doug Liman shot the Casey Affleck crypto drama Bitcoin there. Ayer said he has multiple projects in development that can move to the Grey Box: "As a storyteller half my job is litigating over budget."
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): Ayer is a managing partner in the company that rents the stage he plans to use, so a director who brings his own slate to a cheaper production method can own part of the savings.
The Facts
  • Role: principal and managing partner at ACME AI, involved in operations.
  • ACME AI founder: Ryan Kavanaugh, former Relativity Media co-founder.
  • Technology: "Grey Box," performance transfer; ACME mapped lenses and lighting packages and combined them with models that re-create the physical world.
  • Claimed savings: 50 to 75 percent reduction in time and money versus traveling to a location (ACME's figure).
  • Business model: a dedicated Los Angeles stage, rented to studios "the way many soundstages currently do"; could be replicated elsewhere.
  • Prior use: Doug Liman shot Bitcoin, starring Casey Affleck, largely on the stage despite Australian and other global settings.
  • Peers named by THR: Jon Erwin's Innovative Dreams; Matt Stone and Trey Parker's Deep Voodoo.
  • Crew effect (THR): department heads such as production designers and lighting artists would in many cases be used in a more supervisory role.

YouTube View Counts Now Include People Watching Together on a TV
YouTube began adding estimated co-viewers on TV screens to public view counts for long-form, Shorts and live video; co-views do not change creators' ad revenue or Partner Program eligibility.
YouTube said Monday that public view counts will include "co-views," its statistical estimate of how many people watch a video together on a TV, to align with TV industry standards. It uses no cameras or microphones; the model works from demographic patterns and viewing times. Co-views apply only to new TV views, not retroactively, and do not affect creator ad revenue or Partner Program eligibility. In August YouTube began counting a view as soon as a video starts playing, a change it said would make counts rise faster.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): A creator's public view count now includes YouTube's estimate of people watching together on a TV, which raises the number brands and buyers see while the creator's ad revenue stays on the old count.
The Facts
  • Change: public view counts include estimated "co-views" on TV across long-form videos, Shorts and live content (YouTube update, Monday Nov. 16).
  • Method: a "privacy safe statistical model" using "demographic patterns and viewing times"; no cameras or microphones.
  • Scope: new TV views only; not retroactive.
  • Money: co-views do not affect a creator's ad revenue, YouTube Partner Program eligibility or revenue.
  • Rationale (YouTube): a more "complete picture" and alignment with "TV industry standards."
  • Prior change: in August YouTube began counting a view as soon as a video starts playing.
  • Context (The Verge): YouTube is now more popular on TVs than on phones.

Disney Is Raising Content Spend 9 Percent to $26 Billion, With the New Money Going to Local-Language Series, Sports and Franchise Films
Disney beat on revenue and EPS in its fiscal fourth quarter, guided fiscal 2027 cash content spend up about 9 percent to $26 billion, and said it will stop reporting streaming operating income as a separate line from next quarter.
Disney reported fiscal Q4 2026 revenue of $25.9 billion, up 15.5 percent, and adjusted EPS of $1.77 against $1.68 expected, with an extra 53rd week adding roughly 7 points of revenue growth [R] [2nd]. Streaming had its best quarter: SVOD revenue rose 19 percent to $6.05 billion and SVOD operating income doubled to $824 million [R]. For fiscal 2027 Disney guided cash content spend to about $26 billion, up about 9 percent, driven by sports rights, international programming and feature film production, and it plans to roughly triple local originals for Disney+ over three years [R]. From fiscal Q1 2027 it drops the SVOD operating income disclosure; CFO Hugh Johnston said the change gives "greater flexibility to manage the cost base of the entire portfolio" [R] [call]. A $3 billion efficiency program runs to fiscal 2029, mostly reinvested, and CEO Josh D'Amaro defended licensing Ice Age and Percy Jackson to Netflix on a co-exclusive basis as "additive" [R] [call]. DIS was up about 1.1 percent at midday [2nd].
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): The bigger content budget is aimed at local-language series, sports and franchise films, so international producers gain a better-funded buyer while US talent should expect licensing-revenue definitions to matter more as Disney titles travel to rival platforms.
The Facts
  • Q4 FY26 (14 weeks, ended 10/3/26): revenue $25,947M (+15.5%), total segment operating income $4,970M (+42.8%), adjusted EPS $1.77 vs $1.11 [R]; consensus $1.68 EPS and $25.17B revenue [2nd].
  • FY26: revenue $102.3B (+8.4%), adjusted EPS $7.02 (+18.4%); the 53rd week added about $1.6B of revenue and $0.17 of EPS [R].
  • Entertainment SVOD: revenue $6,050M (+19.1%), operating income $824M vs $402M; FY26 SVOD margin 11.5% [R].
  • FY27 guide: double-digit adjusted EPS growth ex-53rd week, segment OI up about 8%, cash content spend about $26B (+9%), capex about $9B, buybacks about $9B; dividend raised 33% to $2.00 [R].
  • About $3B in annual run-rate savings by FY2029, mostly reinvested; FY26 restructuring and impairment charges $1.46B [R].
  • Titles: Toy Story 5 20M Disney+ views in five days [R] and over $1B global box office [call]; The Devil Wears Prada 2 close to $700M worldwide [call]; The Remarried Empress biggest local original premiere to date [R].
  • Slate: Avengers: Doomsday 12/18, Hexed, Pixar's Gatto in March, Frozen 3 and Lilo & Stitch 2 in FY2028 [R].
  • ESPN holds exclusive rights to the 23-game College Football Playoff from 2027 and carries its first Super Bowl in February 2027 [R] [call].
  • Investor event on long-term strategy set for May 2027 [call].
