UK Actors Would Be Paid Every Time a Digital Replica Is Used Under Equity's New Deal
Equity is recommending its 8,000 actors accept Pact's final offer: consent and payment for each use of a digital replica, a 24% raise on films over £50 million and streamer use fees up three points.
After nearly three years of talks, British actors union Equity is recommending members accept producer body Pact's final offer, Deadline reports. The deal covers most UK film and TV from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2029. Actors must consent to each use of a digital replica, project by project, and are paid when it is used; blanket consent is barred. Equity did not win a right to have replicas deleted. Streaming platform use fees (paid when a show gets a second window on a streamer) rise three percentage points, and the payment period falls from 15 years to 10.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A UK actor's digital replica now carries a fee and a consent right on every project, so a scan made for one production gives the producer nothing it can reuse on the next.
The Facts
  • Parties: Equity (UK actors union, about 8,000 actor members) and Pact (UK producer trade body). Final offer goes to a member vote with a "yes" recommendation, the first time members vote on this agreement.
  • Term: January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2029; covers actors on the majority of British film and TV.
  • AI provisions, four parts: digital replicas, digital alterations of a performance, "Synthetics," and obligations on AI training licensing.
  • Digital replicas: actors "have the right to be paid when your digital replica is used" and "the right to consent" with information on the specific use before consenting. A producer "cannot obtain blanket consent," only consent for specific projects. Substantive changes to scenes agreed in a nudity rider need the actor's approval.
  • Not won: contractual protections for replica deletion, and for digital scanning customarily used for CGI, VFX and SFX.
  • Pay: films budgeted over £50 million ($66 million) +24% over three years (17% in year one); films £30 million to £50 million +13% (7% in year one); TV +9% (3% a year).
  • Streaming platform use fees: +3 percentage points, which Equity says could be a real-terms rise of up to 50%; the period these apply over cut from 15 years to 10.
  • Self-tapes: producers must give 72 hours' notice when sending scripts.
  • Also new: bullying and harassment principles, and a Green Rider on sustainability.
  • Deadline understands the end of streamer "special stipulations" will likely be addressed in Equity's later talks with the US streamers.
  • Quote, Equity General Secretary Paul W Fleming: "We've achieved the best AI provisions in the business."

Michael Mann Is Using Copyright Termination to Reclaim Heat, and New Regency Has Sued
New Regency says Mann wrote Heat as a work for hire and cannot terminate, and its complaint says provisions in both sides' Heat 2 agreements with Amazon depend on the outcome.
Earlier this year Mann served New Regency three termination notices under the Copyright Act provision that lets authors reclaim rights they granted, covering the Heat screenplay and underlying materials, including an alleged 1988 oral agreement from Mann and two companies he controlled. New Regency sued Friday in California federal court to have the screenplay declared a work made for hire (the employer counts as author, and such works cannot be terminated). It says the notices cloud its title and impair its ability to develop, finance and license derivative works. Mann's spokesperson says Heat 2 starts shooting January 19, unaffected.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A writer-director who wrote a property on his own and assigned it later may be able to take it back, so for Heat and its sequels the 1988 paperwork, a work-for-hire commission or a later assignment, decides who owns the franchise.
The Facts
  • Filed: Friday, November 13, 2026, California federal court; New Regency Productions v. Michael Mann; declaratory relief that the Heat screenplay "is not subject to termination."
  • Mann's notices: three, served earlier in 2026; the first sought to terminate all copyright grants for Heat, including an alleged 1988 oral agreement from Mann and two companies he controlled.
  • Per the complaint, Mann told New Regency the assignment was never put in writing and that he only recently discovered the arrangement.
  • New Regency's argument: Mann wrote the screenplay as a work made for hire; works made for hire are generally not eligible for termination.
  • Complaint: "The Termination Notices cloud Regency's title to the Screenplay and impair its ability to develop, finance, and license works derived from it."
  • Complaint: "certain provisions of the agreements that Mann and Regency each entered into with Amazon with respect to Heat 2 depend on the outcome of this litigation."
  • Mann spokesperson: "After 40 years, Michael Mann is exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work"; "confident that the courts will vindicate Michael Mann's statutory rights under the Copyright Act."
  • Heat 2: based on Mann's 2022 novel; shooting begins January 19, 2027, per Mann's statement; the statement says the filing is unrelated to production.
  • Heat (1995): written, produced and directed by Mann.

Filmmakers Can Now Book Theaters Directly Through Attend
John Fithian's Attend Theatrical Marketplace went live at AFM with four films; filmmakers propose terms to theaters, exhibitors post screen rentals and hold lengths, and the platform estimates P&A by location.
The Fithian Group, led by former National Association of Theatre Owners chief John Fithian and Patrick Corcoran, launched Attend at the American Film Market on November 11, IndieWire reports. It opened with Honeyjoon, Mouse, Spoke and Censurada. Filmmakers upload specs, audience data and the social reach of their cast, select theaters the platform recommends and propose terms. Exhibitors list screens, rental prices, four-walling (renting a screen for a flat fee) and hold lengths, and see the box office split before they accept. The platform will open to any filmmaker later.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A filmmaker who already has an audience can now book theaters without paying a distributor's fee, which makes the cast's social reach a booking asset and leaves the marketing spend and its risk with the filmmaker.
The Facts

  • Filmmaker side: runtime, formats, festivals, awards, talent social reach; AI-recommended theaters; per-theater terms; P&A estimates.
  • Exhibitor side: screen specs, rental prices, four-wall options, clean or split screens, hold length, box office share shown before booking; automated invoices and W9s.

Netflix's Share of U.S. Original-Series Viewing Fell to 58 Percent
Luminate counts 13 of Netflix's 25 most-streamed series above 5 billion minutes this year, down from 23 a year ago, and puts its share of original viewing at 58 percent.
A Luminate report by analyst Tyler Aquilina puts Netflix's share of U.S. original-series viewing time at 58 percent, down from more than two-thirds in 2024 and about 60 percent in 2025. Returning hits such as Bridgerton and The Lincoln Lawyer lost viewers in their fourth seasons, and five of Netflix's ten most-watched original seasons this year were limited series or final seasons. New content chief Peter Rice inherits the problem; Netflix declined to comment.

Most Film Editors in an Avid Survey Already Use AI, Mostly for Logging and Search
Of 120 American Cinema Editors members surveyed by Avid, 77.5 percent use AI in post, mainly for transcription, audio cleanup and shot search; 7.5 percent want it assembling rough cuts.
Avid, which sells the Media Composer editing software, surveyed 120 of the American Cinema Editors' 1,200 members. Transcription led at 60 percent, audio cleanup 55 percent and searching footage for specific shots 39.2 percent. Ethical, copyright and security concerns made up nearly half the barriers to use. Emmy-nominated editor Molly Shock said that on MasterChef, AI found a contestant's clock-check shot in seconds, and some half-day tasks now take 15 minutes; she said editors want a say in how the tools are used so the system does not remove "any kind of growth."

  • Survey: Avid; 120 of ACE's 1,200 members; 77.5 percent use AI to some extent in post-production.

LightShed Puts YouTube's Price for Carrying Peacock at About $3 a Subscriber
LightShed estimates YouTube pays about $3 per subscriber a month for Peacock's ad tier inside YouTube Premium, more than 70% below retail, and lets NBCU sell the ads, a first for YouTube.
In a November 11 note, LightShed's Rich Greenfield, Brandon Ross and Mark Kelley argue streamers now either carry other services inside their own app or get carried by one. From early 2027 every U.S. YouTube Premium member gets Peacock's ad tier; LightShed estimates YouTube pays about $3 per subscriber a month, against Peacock's reported $8.40 subscription ARPU (average revenue per user), and says YouTube lets NBCU sell Peacock's ads and shares viewer data it has not given third parties before. Antenna estimated Amazon held at least 49 million channel subscriptions as of June 2026.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): When Peacock reaches tens of millions of new homes at about $3 a head (LightShed's estimate) instead of $8.40, a Peacock show's audience grows while subscription money per viewer falls, and backend tied to subscription revenue may be measured against the smaller number.
The Facts
  • Platform-wide ingestion (LightShed's term): the platform pays a wholesale fee and every member gets the carried service inside the platform's app. Examples: Netflix carrying TF1 in France (since June); Disney+ carrying Channel 4 in the U.K. (early 2027); YouTube Premium carrying Peacock in the U.S. (early 2027).
  • A la carte ingestion (channel stores): Prime Video Channels, Roku Premium Subscriptions, YouTube Primetime Channels; the platform's cut "can run upwards of 25%-30%."
  • LightShed estimate: YouTube pays around $3 per subscriber per month for Peacock's ad-supported tier, "a wholesale haircut of well over 70%" to retail and about a 50% discount to subscription ARPU.
  • NBCU reported Peacock subscription ARPU of $8.40 for Q3 2026 (blend of about 80% ad-tier, 20% ad-free).
  • Per LightShed: YouTube granted NBCU the right to sell ads inside Peacock on YouTube, the first time YouTube has let another company sell ads on its platform, and is providing viewer data it has not shared with third parties before.
  • Antenna: Amazon had at least 49 million channel subscriptions as of June 2026; one-third of new streaming subscriptions come through channel stores.
  • YouTube: 16% of TV time spent, the most-watched platform on TV (per LightShed).
  • Skydance: Ellison said on the Q3 call the company sees value in being "a predominantly direct business" but will decide distribution partnerships partner by partner, naming Amazon and Walmart.
  • Matt Strauss (NBCU Media Group chairman, Decoder podcast): "We need to be an open ecosystem... we're almost indifferent about where somebody consumes the content."

Skydance Said the Warner Bros. Film Slate Will Cost Up to $200 Million in Q4 and Will Greenlight More Selectively
In its first report since closing the Warner Bros. Discovery deal, Skydance said the Warner Bros. film slate underperformed and will cost up to $200 million of Q4 profit, and its 10-Q set out a consent decree that requires 30 to 32 U.S. releases a year with 45-day theatrical windows.
Skydance reported Paramount's standalone Q3 2026: revenue of $7.0 billion, up 5 percent, adjusted EBITDA of $1.0 billion, and Paramount+ revenue up 21 percent on ARPU up about 14 percent [R]. The combined company's story ran the other way at the studio: the letter says the Warner Bros. film slate has underperformed, with a Q4 profit impact of up to $200 million [R], and David Ellison said the fix is the Paramount playbook, "greenlighting more selectively" [call]. The Form 10-Q spells out the states consent decree: for five years, at least 30 to 32 U.S. releases a year with minimums for wide, independent, self-produced and higher-budget films, theatrical windows of at least 45 days, no subscription streaming for at least 90 days, and at least $300 million more a year in U.S. production [R]. All film labels now sit under one leadership team, Jeremy Latcham joins DC Studios, and Paramount+ and HBO Max will be bundled in early 2027 [R] [call]. Gross debt after closing is about $87 billion [R]. The company will stop reporting quarterly subscribers from Q4 [R]. Shares were down about 8.7 percent intraday on 11/10 [2nd].

Elvis Presley's Rights Holders Are Suing Suno Under Tennessee's Voice-Cloning Law
Rights holders of Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records filed two suits against Suno, the Presley suit claiming a violation of Tennessee's ELVIS Act on AI voice cloning.
Both suits claim the AI music company generates music and lyrics that mimic the two artists. The Presley complaint invokes Tennessee's Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer's voice. The Verge reports the suits closely mirror one Jason Isbell and others filed in September, which claimed Suno imitated them without claiming copyright infringement directly. Suno also faces suits from Sony, UMG and Reservoir. Suno says it blocks prompts naming artists and screens uploaded audio and lyrics.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The Presley suit rests on a Tennessee law that treats a singer's voice as a right the estate can enforce apart from any copyright in the songs, and a win could give an artist's voice its own licensing price.
The Facts
  • Plaintiffs: a group of rights holders of Elvis Presley's music; the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records (publisher not named in the readable portion).
  • Claim: Suno illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The Presley suit claims a violation of Tennessee's ELVIS Act (Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security), which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer's voice.
  • Presley complaint: "Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists' identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of cold hard cash." Also: "Suno's ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect."

The Odyssey Carries a No-AI-Training Notice, and Nolan Says Only Studios Can Enforce It
Christopher Nolan, halfway through his first term as DGA president, said on the Hollywood Insiders podcast that the closing boilerplate of The Odyssey bars use of the film as AI training data.
Nolan said it is down to the studios to go after AI copies of films, because with very few exceptions directors do not hold the copyright in the films they make. He said he was very pleased that the end boilerplate of The Odyssey, Universal's release and his current Oscar contender, for the first time carries a message that the film cannot be ingested and used as training data. He argued that AI companies' fair-use defenses will not hold up in court long term, and said directors' residuals depend on how those copyrights are monetized.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Nolan's point is that a director's residuals ride on a copyright the studio owns, so whether a director's film ends up as AI training data is decided by the studio's enforcement, not by anything in the director's own contract.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Christopher Nolan, DGA president (elected September 2025; previously on the guild's Artificial Intelligence Committee). Venue: Hollywood Insiders podcast, reported by Deadline November 7, 2026.
  • On copyright: "With very few exceptions in the Guild, we are not the copyright holders of the films that we've worked on. It's down to the studios to do that."
  • On The Odyssey: "I was very pleased to see that the boilerplate at the end of The Odyssey, for the first time, it contains a message saying that this film cannot be ingested and used as training data."
  • On fair use: AI companies "hide behind fair-use provisions"; "longer term that won't hold up in court. There have already been some significant judgments against it."
  • On residuals (earlier Deadline interview): "our income, our residuals, depends on the appropriate monetization of those copyrights."
  • The Odyssey is a Universal release (Deadline: 52% of its $123.5 million opening came from IMAX and premium large-format screens).

Game Developers Can Now Hire Union Actors for Pitch Demos Before They Are Funded
SAG-AFTRA's Pre-Funding Pitch Interactive Media Agreement, introduced November 5, covers voice and motion work on game demos, vertical slices and prototypes made only to raise production money.
A project qualifies only if it has secured no more than 30% of its initial production funding, and the material cannot feel like a complete game, be sold or be shown publicly; projects that meet only some of those tests can seek a waiver. Hitmarker, reading the published contract, reports that crowdfunding pitches, milestone-funded projects and developers with publishing arrangements are excluded, that pitch session fees are freely negotiable, and that standard Interactive Media Agreement minimums and secondary payments apply if a performance is later used in the finished game.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): An actor on a pitch demo works under a union contract at a negotiated fee, and if the performance carries into the funded game the standard minimums and secondary payments follow it, though the agreement guarantees no role in the finished game.
The Facts
  • Agreement: Pre-Funding Pitch Interactive Media Agreement (SAG-AFTRA), announced November 5, 2026.
  • Covered material: demos, vertical slices, trailers, teasers, sizzle reels or playable prototypes "for the exclusive purpose of soliciting production funding for prospective projects."
  • Eligibility (SAG-AFTRA): no more than 30% of initial production funding secured; the material "must not provide the experience or impression of a complete interactive project"; not commercially released or publicly viewable or playable. Partial fits may seek a waiver via interactive@sagaftra.org.
  • Exclusions (Hitmarker, citing the published contract): crowdfunding pitches (waiver terms possible), projects seeking milestone funding, developers with existing publishing arrangements that provide production funding.
  • Pay (Hitmarker): pitch session fees freely negotiable between performer and developer; if the performance is later used in the finished game, the applicable Interactive Media Agreement terms, minimum session fees and secondary payments apply. No guarantee of employment on the eventual game.
  • Sean Astin, SAG-AFTRA president: the agreement "allows developers to up their game by bringing in professional voice and motion performance talent earlier in the process."
  • Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, national executive director: it "streamlines the hiring of professional union talent."

Twelve Foreign Distributors Pooled Into Lokia to Own the IP, Not Just Buy Territories
Distributors including Wild Bunch Germany, Kazoo Films and Noori Pictures formed Lokia, a Luxembourg company that will develop, finance and license films together as international presales decline.
Distributors from 12 territories formed Lokia ahead of the American Film Market, Deadline reported. Partners keep buying separately for their own markets but plan to develop and produce together, share revenue forecasts, invest in the IP and later acquire as a group. Founder Michael Favelle of Odin's Eye said licensing campaigns for independent animated films are not realistic without worldwide theatrical guarantees before financing. Former Marvel licensing executive Russell Brown is in talks with toy, game and publishing partners, with announcements expected in the fourth quarter. Fintage House will manage collection accounts.

The Facts
  • Lokia: incorporated in Luxembourg; distribution network of buyers from 12 territories, announced November 6, 2026, before AFM.
  • Partners: Wild Bunch Germany and Wild Bunch Austria; Praesens-Film (Switzerland); PRIS Audiovisuals (Portugal); Feelgood Entertainment (Greece); Kazoo Films (UK and Ireland); Noori Pictures (South Korea, Thailand, Vietnam); Filmhouse (Israel); Blitz Group (former Yugoslavia); Donart Film (Czech Republic); Mars Production (Turkey); Horizon Distribution (global airlines and shipping).
  • Plan: develop and produce together, pool market intelligence, pursue licensing and merchandising, later acquire as one entity; partners remain standalone financial entities and keep acquiring individually.
  • Deadline: "a direct response to consolidation in the market and the challenge posed by the declining international pre-sales model."
  • Principals: Michael Favelle (Odin's Eye Entertainment, chief creative officer and president of distribution); Heiko Nemmert (formerly Baby Giant, COO and president of production); Russell Brown (former Marvel Enterprises EVP of worldwide licensing, chief capital and monetisation officer).
  • Lokia OS: partners submit projects, distributors return revenue forecasts, financing and licensing partners see the aggregated picture before capital is committed.
  • Fintage House oversees reporting and collection accounts; co-chairman Robbert Aarts joins the board. Licensing partner announcements expected Q4 2026.
  • Prior groupings cited: Vuelta (2023); foreign distributors financing MadRiver films (2024); producers alliance The Creatives.

Studios Are Banning Employees From Betting on Casting and Release Dates
Studios and production companies have issued guidelines barring staff from prediction-market bets on earnings, casting and release dates, and one company set up an anonymous hotline to report colleagues.
The Hollywood Reporter learned that studios and production companies are quietly telling employees not to bet on prediction markets about studio earnings, casting or release dates, or to pass information to others who bet. PMC, which owns THR, Variety, Deadline and Dick Clark Productions, banned bets on award nominations, casting decisions, production timelines and release dates. BetOnline pulled its James Bond casting market this week after money moved sharply to Callum Turner. Betting on box office receipts is already illegal under the 1958 Onion Futures Act.
Potential Talent Implication: Casting choices and release dates now carry a cash price before they are announced, so everyone on a production with advance knowledge, the talent's own team included, is part of a leak risk studios are now policing.
The Facts
  • Studio guidelines (unnamed companies): no prediction-market bets on studio earnings, casting or release dates; no tipping friends or family; at least one company has an anonymous reporting hotline.
  • PMC handbook update (recent weeks): bans betting on "award nominations, casting decisions, production timelines and release dates."
  • Kalshi disclosed in February that a MrBeast video editor made $5,000 betting on confidential MrBeast content; fired and fined $20,000.

Bruno Dumont Made His Next Feature With Generative AI and No Actors After French Financing Dried Up

Bruno Dumont told Screen International his feature The End was made entirely with generative AI, without actors or a film crew, on what Screen calls a shoestring budget. He wrote the script more than 25 years ago and shelved it because its earthquake and asteroid sequences were too expensive to shoot. He began in August and has wrapped. He is producing independently, with no sales agent yet, and plans festival premieres before distribution. "It is becoming harder and harder to finance films in France," he said. A conventional live-action feature with Bathysphere Films is also in development.

The Facts

  • Method: generative AI for images, performances and sound, made from his Paris home; no actors, no traditional crew. Works scene by scene from his own shot breakdowns; used faces from Flemish paintings as references for characters.

"I'm like a director working with a crew, except that my crew is a machine." "It is becoming harder and harder to finance films in France. Today I have complete freedom."
  • Separately developing a conventionally financed live-action French feature with Nicolas Anthomé's Bathysphere Films.

2026-11-05 Thursday 14 stories

What Talent Needs to Know 10 opportunities · 4 challenges
Opportunities
  • A documentary whose license reverts can now be rebuilt for a fraction of its original cost and sold again, which makes the reversion date and the right to make new versions of the film two of the most valuable terms in a nonfiction license. (Rights Ownership)
  • When one format brings in close to a third of a film's gross, the director who shoots for it is delivering a revenue line, which can give IMAX screen commitments and format exclusivity real weight in a filmmaker's deal. (Project Economics)
  • A single Spider-Man release moved Sony Pictures' quarterly profit more than sixfold, a figure that may carry weight for anyone negotiating on the next Spider-Man film, since the studio's reliance on the franchise is now in its own results. (Project Economics)
  • Sony's record is a film and franchise story while its TV production business shrank, so the open doors at Sony are franchise film and the new anime and live-action adaptation lane, not a bigger TV budget. (Project Economics)
  • With the largest exhibitor healthy and premium screens carrying a third of US admissions, filmmakers who shoot for large formats and filmmakers at Netflix have stronger grounds to ask for premium-screen commitments, full windows and box office bonuses. (Project Economics)
  • When IMAX screens carry nearly a third of a film's gross and streamers buy IMAX-only theatrical runs, an IMAX commitment becomes a deal term worth negotiating, from camera and budget to IMAX weeks and release-date protection. (Project Economics)
  • A horror filmmaker managed by Maxwell or Rowbotham now has a manager who also runs a Lionsgate buyer, so where a project is set up, and on what terms, may need to be shopped against other buyers before Render Road is the answer.
  • Lionsgate now builds its slate on properties it can repeat across film, stage, tours and games, so talent attached to a Lionsgate franchise is attached to more than one revenue line, and the participation terms decide which of those lines it shares in. (New Revenue Stream)
  • A home release no longer ends a big film's theatrical life, so a filmmaker's re-release terms, from format screens to how a second run's grosses count toward box office bonuses, are now worth writing into the deal. (Project Economics)
  • Letterboxd's 30 million monthly users and their ratings would sit with a news publisher rather than a studio, which keeps the largest film word-of-mouth platform outside any one distributor's control.
Challenges & Headwinds
  • With three animation labels under one owner and the Netflix order gone, the label a filmmaker's deal sits at, and the turnaround rights in it, may decide whether a project in development keeps a home.
  • When a buyer treats the theatrical run as marketing for its streaming service, the box office number that usually sets bonuses and backend no longer measures what the film earned the buyer, so the streaming performance terms carry the real value.
  • Because A24 sells foreign rights territory by territory, the overseas gross on an A24 hit mostly stays with regional distributors, which may cap what a filmmaker's backend can draw from it, and a sale would put those deals in a new owner's hands.
  • When one of the town's leading deal lawyers says studio films under $70 million lose money unless they are horror, a mid-budget drama or comedy may need a horror-sized budget, a tentpole's scale or outside financing to get made at a studio.
The Cocaine Cowboys Directors Got Their Film Back From Netflix and Remade It With AI for $200,000
Billy Corben and Alfred Spellman spent about $200,000 using AI to rework nearly 4,000 shots of their 2006 documentary after Netflix's license reverted, and are raising $5 million for a YouTube-first studio.
Rakontur, the Miami company behind Cocaine Cowboys, made documentaries for Netflix, HBO and Hulu until those buyers cut nonfiction spending. Rights to the original film reverted from Netflix this year. Over eight months the directors rebuilt it with ByteDance's Seedance and Google's Veo; the new version premieres on YouTube Nov. 13, and Rakontur expects to recoup through licensing, sponsorships and companion programming rather than YouTube ads alone. Rakontur Direct, with former Complex Networks CEO Rich Antoniello, targets 260 releases a year by its second year and will license shows to streamers only after they premiere on its own channels.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A documentary whose license reverts can now be rebuilt for a fraction of its original cost and sold again, which makes the reversion date and the right to make new versions of the film two of the most valuable terms in a nonfiction license.
The Facts
  • Filmmakers: Billy Corben and Alfred Spellman, Rakontur (Miami), 25 years in business; credits for Netflix (Cocaine Cowboys: The Kings of Miami, 2021), HBO (537 Votes), Hulu (God Forbid), Neon (Men of War), MSNBC Films (From Russia with Lev, Emmy-nominated).
  • Rights: Cocaine Cowboys (2006), licensed to Netflix, reverted to Rakontur in 2026.

  • Recoup plan (Spellman): licensing, sponsorships and related programming, not YouTube ad revenue alone.
  • Rakontur Direct: seeking $5 million from strategic partners for about two years of operation; target 260 releases a year (about five a week) by year two; initial slate short-form, episodes of 15 minutes or less; first series A Sunny Place for Shady People; streamer licensing only after premiere on Rakontur's channels.
  • Hire: Rich Antoniello, co-founder and former CEO of Complex Networks (sold to BuzzFeed for $300 million in 2021).
  • Spellman: Rakontur Direct is "a nonfiction media company that produces original programming, publishes directly to audiences and owns the resulting intellectual property."
  • Spellman: "AI is the third revolution we've lived through in this business."

Ken Ziffren Says Studio Films Under $70 Million Mostly Lose Money Unless They Are Horror
In his annual industry address, Ziffren Brittenham co-founder Ken Ziffren said a pay-one window can bring a studio as much as $250 million, and that wide releases rose to 94 this year.
Ziffren told a ballroom of entertainment lawyers that, outside horror, studio films costing under $70 million tend to lose money, which he said supports a tentpole investment strategy. He said wide releases fell from about 100 before Covid to 75 in 2024 and reached 94 in 2026, with the domestic box office headed to about $10 billion. Downstream, he said, the only distribution costs are remittance taxes, residuals and occasional profit participations. He backed the federal MPTER Act, which he said would bring $10 billion in production, and said AI will lower pre-production, post and production costs.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): When one of the town's leading deal lawyers says studio films under $70 million lose money unless they are horror, a mid-budget drama or comedy may need a horror-sized budget, a tentpole's scale or outside financing to get made at a studio.
The Facts
  • Box office outlook: about $10B domestic and nearly $36B global in 2026, the best since 2019.
  • Wide releases: about 100 pre-Covid, 75 in 2024, 94 in 2026.
  • Ziffren: outside horror, studio films costing under $70M tend to lose money.
  • Downstream: a pay-one window can bring up to $250M; after PVOD, studios license to sister ad-supported services. Quote: "The only costs in distribution are remittance taxes and residuals, and now and then profit participations."
  • MPTER Act (federal production credit, before Senate and House committees): eligible productions over $1M with 75% in the U.S.; Ziffren estimated "$10 billion" for the industry; he hoped it passes in the lame-duck session.
  • AI: will "lower the costs of post and pre-production, and ultimately production itself"; "AI was not a major issue as it was in 2023."

Disney's Startup Program Backed a Gray-Box AI Filmmaking Studio and a Fan Video Tool
Disney's 2026 Accelerator cohort includes Promise, whose gray-box system has AI build sets and props around actors in near real time, and OpenArt, a prompt video app Disney discussed for catalog songs and fan creations.
Disney showed its 2026 Accelerator cohort at a Demo Day in Burbank, TheWrap reported on November 4. Two of the five startups make filmmaking tools. Promise's MUSE system shoots actors in a neutral "gray box" and has AI fill in scenery and props, the method Doug Liman used on Bitcoin: Killing Satoshi; Promise said Disney has no gray-box project in work. OpenArt turns typed prompts into short videos, and Disney discussed it for catalog music videos, marketing and fan creations, screened by a CopySight infringement check. Cohort startups spend 15 weeks working inside Disney divisions.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Disney is testing tools that let marketers and fans generate new video from its catalog, which puts the weight on what existing contracts say about reuse of a performance, a voice or a song in footage nobody shot.
The Facts
  • Disney Accelerator began in 2014 and invests in startups that are further along in maturity; the 2026 cohort has five companies, each spending 15 weeks applying its product inside Disney, much of it at the theme parks.
  • Three cohort members are valued above $1 billion: Simile at $2 billion, FieldAI at $10 billion and Physical Intelligence at $20 billion.
  • Promise Advanced Imagination: AI-native studio; its MUSE operating system supports hybrid "gray box" shooting, where AI fills backgrounds and proxy props with digital scenery in near real time. CEO George Strompolos called gray-box shooting "still pretty cutting edge" and said Disney is not currently working on a gray-box project. Chief creative officer Dave Clark: "this allows me to just focus on the story, focus on the creative, and not worry about having to get my shots in a day."
  • Doug Liman's Bitcoin: Killing Satoshi (Gal Gadot, Pete Davidson, Casey Affleck, Isla Fisher) is cited as the first gray-box AI shoot.
  • OpenArt: prompt-to-video app working across multiple video models; CEO Coco Mao calls conversational instruction "vibe directing." Disney discussed it for new videos for older catalog soundtrack singles, marketing campaigns and user fan creations. It uses a CopySight tool that flags whether generated content risks infringing other IP.
  • TheWrap notes Disney warmed to fan creation after its "ill-fated" deal with OpenAI's Sora.
  • Simile surveys 20,000 to 50,000 people a week, holds a database of one million, and runs virtual focus groups of digital twins; Disney is using it to test its digital booking journey.
  • David Min, VP of corporate innovation: "We're working with the technology to see if it can fit into workflows that we have, so we have the artist involved along the way."
  • CEO Josh D'Amaro: "we'll be very aggressive about this, exploring emerging technologies and seeing how they can support our creators."

Britain Opened a Formal Review of Sky's ITV Deal and Plans to Bring Streaming Under Broadcast Rules
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy issued a public interest notice on Sky's £1.6 billion ($2.2 billion) purchase of ITV's channels and asked Ofcom and the CMA to report back by January 27.
After saying last month she was minded to intervene, Nandy issued a Public Interest Intervention Notice (a formal government review on media plurality grounds) and asked Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority to report by January 27, after which she decides whether to refer the deal to a deeper CMA investigation. A 1994 Contract With Michael Crichton Is Sending The Pitt to a Jury

  • Remaining defendant: Warner Bros. Television, now owned by Skydance. Dismissed: Noah Wyle and executive producers John Wells and R. Scott Gemmill.

The Federal Film Tax Credit Now Depends on a Lame-Duck Congress or a New Democratic One
Supporters of the bipartisan Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act want it on the December 11 funding bill, and three of its Republican cosponsors lost their seats Tuesday.
Lawmakers introduced the bill in September to create the first federal tax credit for U.S. film and TV production. Democrats won both chambers on Tuesday. One insider working on the bill told Deadline the result "makes it harder"; another lobbying source said a blowout beats a close fight, and producer Scott Budnick said the bipartisan support still holds. Sponsor Nathaniel Moran and Rep. Laura Friedman were re-elected; cosponsors Mike Carey, Brian Fitzpatrick and Mariannette Miller-Meeks lost. A Democratic Congress could pass a version alone after January, though one insider put that "probably pretty low" on its list.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Until the bill passes, producers budgeting 2027 shoots are weighing state and foreign incentives against a federal credit that may or may not exist after December 11.
The Facts
  • Bill: the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act (MPTERA), introduced in September; President Trump endorsed such legislation in August.
  • Plan: attach it to the end-of-year funding bill that must pass by December 11 to avoid a shutdown.
  • Re-elected backers: sponsor Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), Rep. Laura Friedman, Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA), Rep. Linda Sánchez (D-CA), Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA).
  • Lost Tuesday: cosponsors Rep. Mike Carey (R-OH), Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA).
  • Friedman: "Every day that passes without a federal film tax credit is another day America remains well behind 65 other countries who are outbidding us for our signature industry."
  • Scott Budnick (1Community): "I think the midterms have little effect on the passage of the Federal credit."
  • Sen. Adam Schiff: "It will take both parties working together to get this across the finish line, and we are pushing hard to make this much-needed incentive a reality."
  • Risks named: Trump withdrawing support or threatening a veto; lame-duck floor time going to nominations; Republican leadership battle after Mike Johnson stepped aside.

Suno Told the Court an Artist's Name Is Just a Genre Label
In its first response to Jason Isbell's class action, Suno argued Tuesday that prompts invoking an artist's name are protected and that no state publicity law bars asking for "a Jason Isbell vibe."
Isbell, David Lowery, Guy Forsyth and Eduardo Calle sued in August, claiming Suno violates state right-of-publicity laws (control over commercial use of a person's identity) by letting users generate tracks that sound like specific artists, including through workarounds such as spacing out a name. Unlike the copyright suits Suno has faced and settled, this case rests on identity, which the plaintiffs say an artist keeps even after a catalog settlement or a training opt-in. Suno's attorney Andrew Gass called the theory a "shadow state law IP regime" that conflicts with federal law, which does not protect an artistic style.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): If identity claims survive where copyright claims settled, an artist's name and voice become an asset separate from the catalog, one a label or AI licensing deal does not automatically cover.
The Facts
  • Plaintiffs: Jason Isbell, David Lowery, Guy Forsyth, Eduardo Calle; federal class action filed August 2026.
  • Claim: Suno violates state publicity laws and keeps artist "voiceprints" users can reach through prompts for "tone and phrasing," real names instead of stage names (the rapper Common), or spaced-out names ("t a y l o r s w i f t").
  • Suno's motion to dismiss, filed Tuesday (attorney Andrew Gass): "Congress made the considered policy choice not to confer intellectual property protection on an artistic style, precisely to allow subsequent creators to build on the prior works of a genre."
  • Suno: invoking an artist's name to describe a genre is protected by the First Amendment. "No state confers a right of publicity that prohibits a musician in a studio from saying to their producer, 'let's go for something here with more of a Jason Isbell vibe.'"
  • Distinction: other suits against Suno were copyright claims, several of which ended in settlements; this one argues identity rights survive those settlements and any training opt-in.
  • Plaintiffs' attorney did not respond to Variety.

Opportunities
  • Sony bought into a rival studio's film to keep working with the director of its biggest movie, so a record grosser can bring a second studio's money and distribution into a filmmaker's next project. (Project Economics)
  • Kazan had a soft opening and a hit by week four, and Netflix answered with "Lonesome Dove," so a showrunner's standing at Netflix may rest on how a series grows after launch as much as on its first-week number.

  • Netflix is paying for daily, lean-back formats it does not make itself, so a creator with a talk show, video podcast or kids series can sell Netflix on daytime use while keeping an audience on YouTube. (New Revenue Stream)
  • Fox's record profits come from sports, news and political ads rather than entertainment, so the growing buyer inside Fox for library, originals and creator content is Tubi, at budgets set by ad revenue. (Project Economics)
  • A drama sold to Paramount+ before the merger could premiere on HBO under a different executive, so for producers in that pipeline the platform, the brand and the person giving notes are all open again.

Challenges & Headwinds
  • Disney is cutting staff inside the studio and the TV networks while saying part of the savings goes back into film and TV programming, so the content budget may hold even as the executives who buy for it change.
  • The chain drew its line at the window, not at Netflix, so the length of the theatrical window may decide how many screens a filmmaker's streamer-financed film gets, and Apple may soon be a second streamer buying with theaters in the deal.

  • Apple's awards record gives talent on its shows strong standing in renewals and new deals, but a company absorbing record component costs is more likely to hold Apple TV spending steady than to grow it.

Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): The chain drew its line at the window, not at Netflix, so the length of the theatrical window may decide how many screens a filmmaker's streamer-financed film gets, and Apple may soon be a second streamer buying with theaters in the deal.
The Facts

What Talent Needs to Know 7 opportunities · 4 challenges
Opportunities
  • If above-the-line pay becomes eligible, a large star or director salary could stop counting against a California shoot and become part of what the state helps pay for. (Project Economics)
  • Druski paid for his own sketches and kept them, and Netflix is now paying to license that library on top of an exclusive deal for new shows. (Rights Ownership)
  • WME is now on the record that a paid market for training on its clients' work already exists, and the open question is whether the court treats that market as one OpenAI was obliged to use. (New Revenue Stream)
  • Netflix put a theatrical release into the announcement of a finished auteur film it bought worldwide, a precedent sellers of comparable films may cite while its film leadership is being replaced.
  • California's credit does not cover what actors and directors are paid, and adding those salaries, as one lawmaker proposed, would change the math most for productions with large above-the-line budgets. (Project Economics)
  • A headset release after theaters is now a separate window a studio can license on a franchise film, and the open question for anyone with backend is whether money from that window counts toward their participation. (New Revenue Stream)
  • An independent animated feature with no shot at a weekend booking now has a buyer that acquires films worldwide and is offering 26 theatrical slots a year in the hours the studios do not use. (Company Building)
Challenges & Headwinds
  • The company that owns "Spaced" could remaster it with AI and put it on sale without asking the director or the creators, and nothing reported so far says their deals gave them a say over a new master.
  • Producers making Netflix shows in London, Europe, Latin America and Asia have lost the executive who ran physical production on them, and no successor has been named.
  • Producers and writers holding overall or first-look deals at both Paramount and Warner Bros. sit in the overlap the analysts named first, so the renewal and opt-out dates on those deals may matter more this year than the size of the guarantee.
  • The two halves of Topjaw now sit at different agencies, and any new Topjaw deal, from a channel sponsor to a network order, could have two representatives from two firms at the table.
Newsom Proposed a $1 Billion Film Credit That Would Cover Talent Salaries
Gov. Gavin Newsom proposed lifting California's annual film and TV credit from $750 million to at least $1 billion, opening it to above-the-line pay and extending it through 2040.
Newsom's Nov. 2 proposal raises the program to at least $1 billion a year and extends eligibility to above-the-line compensation (pay for actors, directors, writers and producers), subject to funding caps. It also reserves $100 million a year for independent productions, up $26 million, adds a 5% credit boost for companies committing to at least two California productions, and moves the sunset from 2030 to 2040. The push will fall to the next governor and the Legislature, THR reported. ProdPro data cited by THR has New York production spending up 87% in the latest quarter against California's 17%.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): If above-the-line pay becomes eligible, a large star or director salary could stop counting against a California shoot and become part of what the state helps pay for.
The Facts
  • Proposal (governor's release, Nov. 2): annual credit from $750 million to "at least" $1 billion; above-the-line talent compensation eligible, "subject to funding caps"; $100 million a year for independent productions (up $26 million); 5% credit boost for companies committing to at least two distinct qualifying California productions; sunset extended from five years to 10, through 2040.
  • Last year's expansion took the credit from $330 million to $750 million ($3.75 billion over five years through 2030). In its first expanded year, per the release: applications up 82%, $8.25 billion in direct production spending, film shoot days up 52%, TV shoot days up more than 7%, more than 43,000 cast and crew jobs.
  • Newsom asked Congress to pass the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act (MPTERA) by year end and backed a 20% federal credit that would stack with state programs.
  • Newsom: "At least $1 billion in tax credits means more investment flowing into our economy and more opportunity across the industry... But states can't shoulder the cost alone."
  • THR: the follow-through falls to the next governor, likely Xavier Becerra if he defeats Steve Hilton on Nov. 3.
  • ProdPro (October report, via THR): California $6.06 billion in production spend over 12 months vs. New York $4.63 billion; New York up 87% in the latest quarter vs. California 17%; New York had 17 live-action features budgeted over $10 million shooting last quarter vs. 13 for California.
  • Recent credits (Oct. 7 round, via THR): untitled Pixar animated feature $40.1 million, Lionsgate's "Michael" sequel $30.8 million, untitled Paramount crime thriller $29.3 million; "The Pitt" $24.2 million.
  • California Film Commission director Colleen Bell (outgoing) and Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur both backed the call.
  • Recently signed state law also adds a post-production credit, disclosure rules for ads using AI-generated performers, and stronger digital likeness protections including for deceased performers.

WME Told the OpenAI Court That AI Training Should Be Licensed, Not Stopped
WME's Oct. 30 amicus brief in the New York Times case against OpenAI says creators should decide whether, and on what terms, their work trains AI, and cites 28 paid data deals.
WME filed an amicus brief (a friend-of-the-court filing) on Oct. 30 in the consolidated copyright case brought by the New York Times and others against OpenAI. The agency's position is that AI use of creative work "should be licensed," not stopped, and that any use affecting talent's rights needs compensation and authorization. The brief cites at least 28 paid training-data deals between mid-2023 and mid-2024 and says AI developers are now shopping for licenses to film and TV libraries. SAG-AFTRA, the AFM and both WGAs filed a joint brief on Oct. 29; the Justice Department backed OpenAI in September.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): WME is now on the record that a paid market for training on its clients' work already exists, and the open question is whether the court treats that market as one OpenAI was obliged to use.
The Facts
  • Filed: Oct. 30, 2026, amicus brief by WME Group legal chief Courtney Braun and outside firm Jayaram PLLC; 18 pages (Deadline).
  • WME: "WME's position is therefore not that AI use of creative materials should be stopped, but that it should be licensed."
  • WME: "any use of AI that affects talents' and creators' rights must come with proper compensation and authorization"; it "seeks to preserve the legal framework that lets creators decide whether, and on what terms, their protected work is used to develop or train AI systems."
  • Brief: between mid-2023 and mid-2024, more than two dozen licensing deals or partnerships were announced, at least 28 involving payment for training data, including News Corp's reported five-year, $250 million agreement with OpenAI, Reddit's $60 million deal with Google, and Shutterstock's reported $25 million to $50 million deals with each of Apple, Amazon and Google.
  • Brief: "that market has grown as AI developers continue to actively shop for licenses to film and television libraries."
  • Deadline calls WME the first major Hollywood agency to enter this case. SAG-AFTRA, the American Federation of Musicians and the WGA East and West filed a joint brief Oct. 29.
  • The Justice Department filed in September: "The United States has a strong interest in this Court rejecting any argument that training LLMs on copyrighted texts violates copyright law."
  • The case is nearly three years old; the Times alleges OpenAI built "substitutive products without permission or payment."

California Lawmakers Floated a Tax Credit on Actor and Director Salaries
At an Oct. 29 Assembly hearing, members discussed lifting the $750 million cap on California's film credit and subsidizing above-the-line pay, which the program now excludes.
An Assembly select committee met in North Hollywood on Oct. 29 to discuss removing the cap on California's $750 million film and TV credit, which projects compete for in periodic windows. Chair Rick Chavez Zbur said he wants to raise or eliminate the cap next session but called it "a heavy lift" given the state deficit. Assemblyman Nick Schultz floated extending the program past its 2030 sunset and subsidizing above-the-line costs (salaries for actors, directors and other key creatives). Betsy Beers testified that a "Grey's Anatomy" spinoff lost out on the credit and is shooting in Albuquerque.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): California's credit does not cover what actors and directors are paid, and adding those salaries, as one lawmaker proposed, would change the math most for productions with large above-the-line budgets.
The Facts
  • Hearing: Assembly Select Committee on Growing and Retaining the Creative Economy in California, North Hollywood, Oct. 29 (Variety).
  • Program: $750 million annual cap; base credit raised from 20% to 35% last year; cap raised from $330 million; sunsets in 2030. Projects apply in windows and are ranked on a "jobs ratio" score.
  • Rick Chavez Zbur (chair): "I think either increasing the cap or eliminating it... But you know that is a heavy lift." He floated "dynamic scoring" of the credit's return.
  • Nick Schultz floated extending the sunset date, subsidizing above-the-line costs (salaries for actors, directors, etc.), and opening eligibility to commercials and game shows.
  • Betsy Beers (Shondaland): a "Grey's Anatomy" spinoff set in West Texas did not get the credit in two tries (scored too low, then the program was oversubscribed); "now we are filming in Albuquerque."
  • Georgia's credit has no limit; New York can borrow from future-year allocations.
  • Legislative Analyst's Office economist Rowan Isaaks: research shows film credits return 20 to 50 cents per state dollar; a more generous credit "might mean fewer projects overall." LAEDC (MPA-funded study): $1.07 return.
  • FilmLA: LA-area production volume continues to fall even as the share of scripted shows with a state subsidy has nearly doubled. Congress is considering a 20% national incentive.

That would be 6.3% above 2025 and the best year since 2019's $42.3 billion. International markets outside China would rise about 14% to $19.7 billion. Five films have passed $1 billion, led by Spider-Man: Brand New Day at $2.5 billion and The Odyssey at $1.8 billion, while two indie horror films broke out: Obsession at $525 million and Backrooms at $400.6 million.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): With North America up 18% and two indie horror films past $400 million worldwide, box office bonuses and theatrical backend may again be worth more on a mid-budget original than a streaming buyout.
The Facts
  • Gower Street 2026 global forecast: $35.7B, up 2.9% from its April (CinemaCon) estimate; based on Rentrak actuals and Gower estimates.
  • Versus 2025: +6.3%. Best since 2019 ($42.3B).
  • Split: North America $10.5B (+18% vs 2025); international excluding China $19.7B (nearly +14%); China $5.5B (about -26%; admissions and ticket prices down).
  • Billion-dollar titles in 2026: Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($2.5B), The Odyssey ($1.8B), Toy Story 5, Michael ($1B), Super Mario Galaxy Movie ($1B).
  • Indie horror: Obsession ($525M), Backrooms ($400.6M).
  • China local hits: Pegasus 3 (near $654M), Once Upon a Time in the Middle East ($356M), Kung Fu Soccer ($349M).
  • Summer 2026: North American record of $4.76B per Rentrak; global summer $14.5B, best since 2019's $14.9B.
  • Still to come in 2026: Godzilla Minus Zero, The Cat in the Hat, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Focker-in-Law, Hexed, Dune: Part Three, Avengers: Doomsday, Jumanji: Open World.

HBO Shot Big Little Lies for One Day to Keep Its California Tax Credit
Big Little Lies season 3 filmed for one day on Thursday at Warner Bros.' Burbank Ranch lot; full production is not expected until next year and has no locked date.
Variety, citing insiders, reports the single day of principal photography was held so the show keeps its already-approved California tax credit. State rules require principal photography to begin within 180 days of the Conditional Allocation Letter (the state's credit approval), or 240 days for projects spending $100 million or more; when the show received its letter is unclear. A DGA-approved director already involved with the series was on set, though no season 3 director is confirmed. HBO declined comment. Executive producer David E. Kelley shot the first two seasons in California without incentives.

The Facts

  • Full production: expected next year; no date locked (Variety, insiders).
  • Reason per insiders: to maintain the show's approved California tax credit.
  • California rule cited by Variety: principal photography must begin within 180 calendar days of the Conditional Allocation Letter date, or 240 days for a qualified expenditure budget of $100M or more.

  • Creative: Francesca Sloane (Mr. and Mrs. Smith) writing episode 1 and executive producing with David E. Kelley, Nicole Kidman and Reese Witherspoon; Liane Moriarty's August novel Big Little Truths expected to be the basis of season 3.

Anime Production Houses Now Take Equity in Their Shows to Share in $16 Billion of Overseas Sales
Overseas sales reached $16.1 billion of Japan's $28.18 billion anime business in 2025, but only $3.2 billion flowed back to the companies that make the shows.
Japan's anime industry grew 15.8% to $28.18 billion in 2025, according to the Association of Japanese Animations (AJA), presented at TIFFCOM. Overseas revenue rose 17% to $16.1 billion, about 57% of the total; domestic revenue rose just over 14% to $12 billion. Revenue reaching production companies, as distinct from the production committees (the investor groups that finance and own most anime), rose 8% to $3.2 billion. AJA's Masahiro Hasegawa said more production companies now take an equity position in their works to keep the IP and share in overseas revenue.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The companies that make anime collect about $3.2 billion of a $28 billion business, and the route to a larger share is equity in the title itself, which carries the overseas revenue a production fee never touches.
The Facts
  • Japan anime industry 2025: $28.18 billion (JPY4.45 trillion), up 15.8% (AJA Anime Industry Report, presented at TIFFCOM).
  • Overseas revenue: $16.1 billion (JPY2.54 trillion), about 57% of the total, up 17%. Domestic: $12 billion (JPY1.9 trillion), 43%, up just over 14%.
  • 2024 comparison: overseas sales grew 26% while domestic was mostly flat. Overseas first overtook domestic in 2020.
  • Revenue flowing back to anime production companies (not production committees): $3.2 billion (JPY505 billion) in 2025 vs $2.95 billion (JPY466 billion) in 2024, up 8%.
  • Masahiro Hasegawa, editor-in-chief of AJA's Anime Industry Report: more production companies are taking an equity position in their works, holding on to IP and participating in overseas revenue.
  • Demon Slayer: Kimetsu No Yaiba The Movie, Infinity Castle grossed about $800 million worldwide in 2025, the highest-grossing Japanese film of all time. Chiikawa The Movie has grossed about $159 million worldwide in 2026.
  • Japan's IP360 initiative targets $127 billion (JPY20 trillion) in content exports by 2033, including $38 billion (JPY6 trillion) for anime.

CAA and Hollywood Stars Told the OpenAI Court a Licensing Market for Their Work Already Exists
The Human Consent Foundation, CAA and voice-actor and music groups filed a 31-page brief in The New York Times case against OpenAI and Microsoft, signed by stars including Scarlett Johansson, Robert De Niro and Julia Roberts.
The Human Consent Foundation, a nonprofit Cate Blanchett co-founded, filed an amicus brief (an outside party's argument to the court) on Friday in the Southern District of New York, joined by CAA, the Music Artists Coalition, the National Association of Voice Actors, Writer, Inc and the Creative Coalition on AI. It answers OpenAI and Microsoft's claim that licensing training data is cost-prohibitive and impossible to value: "The creative industries already have in place a proven infrastructure and workflows to clear rights for dispersed works at scale." OpenAI points to briefs backing fair use, including one from the U.S. government.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Whether a court accepts that a working market for licensing a face, voice or script already exists decides whether AI training is something talent gets paid for or something talent cannot stop.
The Facts
  • Filed: late Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, Southern District of New York, in The New York Times v. OpenAI and Microsoft (suit filed December 2023; the Times moved for summary judgment last month).
  • Filers: Human Consent Foundation (founded as RSL Media in May by Nikki Hexum and Cate Blanchett; registry launched in June; backed by Steven Soderbergh), joined by CAA, Music Artists Coalition, National Association of Voice Actors, Writer, Inc, Creative Coalition on AI.
  • Appendix signatories include Anne Hathaway, Emma Thompson, Dan Levy, Ron Howard, Madonna, Olivia Wilde, Ariana DeBose, Bette Midler, Christine Vachon, Helen Mirren, Dave Eggers, Greg Berlanti, Julia Roberts, Paul Feig, Ram Bergman, Rian Johnson, Robert De Niro, Rosario Dawson, Scarlett Johansson, Vince Gilligan and the Stan Lee Foundation.
  • Brief: "Defendants have argued that licensing creative works for AI training is cost-prohibitive... The creative industries already have in place a proven infrastructure and workflows to clear rights for dispersed works at scale and cost-effectively."
  • Blanchett: "If someone wants to use my face, my voice or my image, they ask me first. There is a contract. There is a conversation."
  • Hexum: "There is already a functioning market and infrastructure for licensing creative work."
  • OpenAI cited a Friday blog post listing briefs in support of fair use, including from the U.S. government (as of last month). Microsoft did not respond.
  • Day earlier: SAG-AFTRA, WGA and AFM brief said fair use "would render moot the terms the unions and the industry agreed to at the bargaining table" (filed 10/29).

Marcus Says an Early Home Release Wins Few Extra Rentals and Costs Box Office
Greg Marcus cited industry data that the same customers rent a film whether it reaches homes in week two or week eight, and asked studios to stop home-release ads during theatrical runs.
Marcus Corp. chairman and CEO Greg Marcus said on the company's third-quarter call and to Deadline that the propensity to buy a $20 to $25 premium home rental is about the same from week two through week eight. His argument: studios lose few rentals by waiting and gain theatrical box office. He also asked studios to hold "available at home" marketing until a film's exclusive run ends. Universal has promised a 45-day exclusive window for major releases from 2027, and Skydance has committed to 45-day and 90-day windows with limits on home-viewing marketing.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): If rentals hold at week eight, an early home release mainly moves money out of the theatrical gross, which is the number most backend and box office bonuses are paid on.
The Facts
  • Greg Marcus, chairman and CEO, Marcus Corp., on the Q3 call: "The propensity to buy transactional video on demand at that price really is about the same in week 2 through week 8."
  • PVOD/TVOD generally follows theatrical at about 45 days; Marcus put the rental price at $20 to $25 for a couple of days. Consensus window to SVOD is about 90 days; Marcus wants it longer.
  • Marcus: "available at home" emails during the run send "a message you should wait" and are "very, very deleterious."
  • Windows by studio (Deadline): Disney's are the longest; Universal promised a 45-day exclusive theatrical window for all major releases starting in 2027; Skydance committed to 45-day PVOD and 90-day SVOD windows with restrictions on marketing home viewing.
  • Marcus Corp. reported a record third quarter, which Marcus credited in large part to younger audiences returning to cinemas. He said he wants more dramas and comedies to bring older audiences back.

Flawless's AI Dubbing Tools, Built on Actor Consent, Were Sold in a UK Insolvency
Administrator BTG sold the TrueSync dubbing and DeepEditor tools to TBellScout, a startup owned by Elastic founder Steven Schuurman, after Flawless Holdings filed for administration this month.
Flawless raised $100 million from wealthy individuals to build AI dubbing tools endorsed by SAG-AFTRA and used on hundreds of Hollywood productions, including Fall and Watch the Skies. Its UK company, Flawless Holdings, filed for administration (the UK equivalent of Chapter 11, run by an outside insolvency firm) earlier in October. BTG, appointed by lender Sprk Capital, sold TrueSync and DeepEditor to TBellScout, owned by Dutch billionaire Steven Schuurman, who confirmed the deal to Deadline. Co-founders Scott Mann and Nick Lynes still control Flawless AI Inc., the U.S. company that held the studio relationships.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Flawless's consent-based approach lived in its studio relationships, and the tools have gone to a buyer without those relationships, so the protection that travels with a dubbed performance is the AI language in the actor's own contract.
The Facts
  • Flawless spent $100 million, raised from wealthy individuals rather than venture capital, building SAG-AFTRA-endorsed AI dubbing technology.
  • Assets sold: TrueSync (visual dubbing; named one of Time's Best Inventions) and DeepEditor (AI post-production; changes dialogue and performance without reshoots). Buyer: TBellScout, owned by Steven Schuurman, founder of Elastic. Schuurman confirmed the acquisition and declined further comment.
  • Seller: Flawless Holdings Limited (UK trading company, founded 2020), which filed for administration earlier in October. Administrator BTG was appointed by Sprk Capital, a UK tech lender holding fixed and floating charges over Flawless.
  • Flawless's third tool, the rights management platform Artistic Rights Treasury, is not named among the assets sold.
  • Scott Mann and Nick Lynes remain in control of Flawless AI Inc., the U.S. business that built the studio relationships on a consent-based approach; they are said to be exploring a new venture. Amit Kapur became co-CEO in March.
  • Credits: Fall (AI used to remove swearing for a PG-13), Watch the Skies (first theatrical feature with immersive AI dubbing, released with XYZ Films), The Book of Solutions, Tatami, Smugglers, Vincent Must Die, The Light. Studios have largely declined to disclose their AI use.

Voicemod, an AI voice-modifying platform, said Friday it will add soundboards from Star Wars and Marvel projects under a deal with Disney. Users play quotes and sound effects as reactions on social and gaming platforms; Variety reports the tools do not appear to let users make their own voices sound like the characters. Meta's New Business Terms Would Let It Scrape Business Accounts for Its Products With No Opt-Out
The Copyright Alliance called the terms "unconscionable," a court in Oslo temporarily barred them, and Meta said the Nov. 20 start could slip again pending industry consultation.
Meta's updated business terms would apply to commercial accounts on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads and WhatsApp. The current draft lets Meta use scrapers and crawlers "to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products"; an earlier draft also said "train" and was revised after publisher pushback. The Copyright Alliance, whose members include the RIAA, NMPA, Universal Music Group, ASCAP and BMI, said the terms still allow broad scraping for generative AI, let Meta ignore robots.txt (the standard do-not-crawl signal), and offer no opt-out. Meta says content owners can still use robots.txt.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Every production company and creator brand runs a Meta business account, so if these terms take effect, keeping work out of Meta's products could come down to closing the account.
The Facts
  • Terms: updated commercial terms for business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads, WhatsApp; effective date moved from Oct. 30 to Nov. 20 on Oct. 23; Meta now says the consultation "could extend beyond November 20, in which case we'd delay implementation." Reuters reported an indefinite delay.
  • Earlier draft (reported by Nieman Lab Oct. 15): Meta "may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of" its products. Current draft drops "train."
  • Copyright Alliance (Oct. 27), CEO Keith Kupferschmid: the terms "could allow Meta to scrape any business user's content and use that scraped content, much of which is protected by copyright, in Meta's own business products, including for advertising, and to train and ground the company's AI products." No opt-out; accept or terminate the account.
  • Meta (Andy Stone, VP Communications, Oct. 28): "We do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders." To Reuters: "content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences."
  • Oslo court (Oct. 28) temporarily barred implementation on a challenge from ten Norwegian media groups including NRK and Schibsted, pending a final ruling.
  • Earlier complaints from publishers and advertisers to EU and UK antitrust authorities (Reuters).
  • Letters: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (Oct. 23) and Sen. Adam Schiff (Oct. 24).
  • Copyright Alliance says it represents more than two million individual creators and 15,000 organizations.

About 30 people are out, and the rest now work on film, TV, the book club and the marketing and partnerships around them, Deadline reports.

Business Insider reports offers of $50,000 to some creators and podcasters, scaling to $500,000 in some deals, all non-exclusive, while Adam Mosseri calls existing creator payments "R.O.I. negative."
Meta is testing Features, an Instagram tab for videos up to 90 minutes. Puck's Julia Alexander writes that Instagram has no preroll or mid-roll ads and no revenue-share program like YouTube's; Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri and product VP Tessa Lyons say there are no plans to add those ad formats, and Mosseri has not committed to sharing revenue. Amazon Said Prime Video Is Now Profitable, With Revenue in the Tens of Billions
Andy Jassy told investors Prime Video is "now profitable in its own right" at a revenue run rate in the tens of billions, and Amazon MGM Studios has passed $1.2 billion in 2026 box office, in a quarter where the stock fell about 6 percent after hours on an EPS miss and a $220 billion AI capex year.
Amazon reported Q3 revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12 percent [R], and record operating income of $28.1 billion at a 13.9 percent margin [R], but EPS of $1.89 missed the $1.96 consensus [R]/[2nd] and the stock fell about 6.1 percent after hours [2nd]. Inside the call, Jassy said "Prime Video has emerged as a significant business with a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars, now profitable in its own right" [call]. The release adds that Amazon MGM Studios has exceeded $1.2 billion in global box office this year on Project Hail Mary and Verity, that Thursday Night Football is averaging 17.7 million viewers in its best start ever, and that Reacher season four drew 66 million viewers in 28 days [R]. Video and music expense rose 7 percent to $5.9 billion in the quarter, against 20 percent over nine months [R]. Advertising grew 11 percent to $19.6 billion on a Prime Day timing shift, with high-teens growth guided for Q4 [R]. Capex stays at about $220 billion for 2026 and will be higher in 2027 [R]/[call], and trailing free cash flow is an outflow of $42.4 billion [R].
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A buyer that has now told investors its video business is profitable will price new deals to protect that line, so talent with proven franchises, sports-adjacent formats or a box office record has the leverage at Amazon, and everyone else should expect harder questions on cost.
The Facts
  • Q3 2026: net sales $201.9B (+12%) [R]; operating income $28.1B vs $17.4B, 13.9% margin [R]; EPS $1.89 vs ~$1.96 consensus [R]/[2nd].
  • AWS: $46.0B (+39%), operating income $17.8B, $184B run rate [R]; growth "north of 40%" guided for 2027 and 2028 [call].
  • Prime Video: revenue run rate "in the tens of billions," "now profitable" [call]; no segment P&L disclosed.
  • Amazon MGM Studios: more than $1.2B global box office in 2026 to date (Project Hail Mary, Verity) [R].
  • TNF 17.7M average viewers through six games (+16%); NBA season two opener 2M+ US viewers; Reacher S4 66M in 28 days [R].
  • Video and music expense $5.9B in Q3 (+7%), $18.8B over nine months (+20%) [R, 10-Q].
  • Advertising $19.6B (+11%), subscription services $14.0B (+11%) [R]; Q4 ad growth guided to the high teens [R].
  • 2026 cash capex ~$220B [R]; Q3 cash capex $75.9B [call]; trailing free cash flow outflow $42.4B [R].
  • AMZN about -6.1% after hours on 10/29, to $228.90 [2nd].

What Talent Needs to Know 5 opportunities · 6 challenges
Opportunities
  • A producer who kept the international rights to a Japanese, Korean, French or Turkish series owns the kind of title that now makes up at least half of what Netflix and Disney+ acquire. (Rights Ownership)
  • HBO kept buying through Skydance's first month, and five of the seven new projects began with a title someone already owned; for now, whoever controls a known title may have the easier conversation there than a writer arriving with only an original. (Rights Ownership)
  • Marcus sold 17 percent more tickets while raising prices only 4.3 percent, and growth that comes from more people in seats is the kind that reaches a deal paid on box office. (Project Economics)
  • RedBird already backs Ben Affleck and Matt Damon's Artists Equity, and its new $1 billion pool with Oseary is one more source of equity for a talent-founded company that sits between media and technology. (Company Building)
  • A creator with a free YouTube show now has a theatrical window to offer: Dimoldenberg's final episode plays in cinemas three days before it posts online, with YouTube's own Cine Club booking the screens. (New Revenue Stream)
Challenges & Headwinds
  • When a studio judges a theatrical run by the awareness it builds for streaming and publishes no grosses, a box office bonus has nothing to trigger, and the value may move to how the Prime Video performance is defined and reported.
  • The AI terms the guilds won in 2026 pay off only if training needs a license, so whether actors and writers are ever paid when their work trains a model may turn on this ruling as much as on any contract.
  • Amazon now calls Prime Video profitable on tens of billions in revenue but publishes no figures for it, so talent with bonuses or backend on Amazon titles is paid against numbers only Amazon can see.
  • A Netflix order pays the budget but takes every territory, so a European producer gives up the international sales a broadcaster deal would allow, a trade that costs most on shows Netflix stops after one or two seasons.
  • Starz now wants to own what it airs and to pay less per episode for it, so a producer selling Starz an original series is selling the copyright and the downstream revenue that comes with it.
  • Row K bought four Toronto films on undisclosed backing and released two before freezing distribution, so a filmmaker selling to a new distributor is protected by a minimum guarantee paid at signing and rights that revert if no release comes.

The Guilds Told the OpenAI Court a Fair Use Ruling Would Void Their AI Licensing Terms
SAG-AFTRA, the WGA East and West and the AFM filed a 34-page amicus brief Thursday in the New York copyright case against OpenAI, citing the AI bargaining right they won this year.
The four unions asked the federal court hearing the consolidated case brought by the New York Times, other outlets and authors including George R.R. Martin and John Grisham to reject a categorical fair use exemption (a blanket legal permission) for training AI models. The brief says the 2026 contracts gave writers and actors a notice-and-bargaining right over third-party licenses of covered work for AI training, and that a ruling that training is fair use "would render moot the terms the unions and the industry agreed to at the bargaining table." Fair use, the unions argue, must stay a case-by-case call.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The AI terms the guilds won in 2026 pay off only if training needs a license, so whether actors and writers are ever paid when their work trains a model may turn on this ruling as much as on any contract.
The Facts
  • Filers: SAG-AFTRA, the American Federation of Musicians, the Writers Guild of America East and West. Joint amicus brief, filed Thursday, October 29, 2026; 34 pages.
  • Case: consolidated copyright action in New York federal court against OpenAI. Plaintiffs include the New York Times, Florida and Arkansas papers, The Intercept, Sarah Silverman, the Authors Guild, and authors Ta-Nehisi Coates, George R.R. Martin, John Grisham, Michael Connelly, Jonathan Franzen and Jodi Picoult, among others.
  • Ask: reject a categorical fair use exemption for AI training; decide fair use case by case.
  • Brief: "The harms of unlicensed training fall not just on companies like the News Plaintiffs, but on the countless professionals behind the work."
  • Brief: a blanket exemption would allow a "potentially enormous transfer of value" from creators to corporations.
  • Contract hook: in 2026 negotiations the writers and actors guilds won a notice-and-bargaining right for third-party licenses of covered work used to train commercial generative AI systems.
  • Brief: "These negotiated provisions presuppose that training on covered work is a use that can be licensed and that the people whose work is used have a stake in the terms."

Amazon does not break out Prime Video's financials or subscribers. Jassy credited Reacher, The Boys, Fallout and Project Hail Mary, plus Thursday Night Football, which averaged 17.7 million viewers through six games, up 16%. Amazon MGM Studios has passed $1.2 billion in global box office in 2026.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Amazon now calls Prime Video profitable on tens of billions in revenue but publishes no figures for it, so talent with bonuses or backend on Amazon titles is paid against numbers only Amazon can see.
The Facts
  • Source: Amazon Q3 2026 earnings call, Thursday, October 29, 2026; CEO Andy Jassy.
  • Prime Video revenue run rate: "tens of billions" of dollars; "profitable in its own right" (reiterated). No separate financials or subscriber counts disclosed.
  • Ad tier: over 315 million monthly active users worldwide, more than 130 million in the U.S.; ad-free upgrade $4.99 a month.
  • Subscription segment net sales (Prime fees, video, music, other non-AWS subscriptions): up 12% to $14 billion. Advertising services: up 12% to $19.64 billion.
  • Thursday Night Football: 17.7 million average viewers through six games, up 16% on last season's average. NBA season opener doubleheader: over 2 million U.S. viewers.
  • Reacher season 4: 66 million viewers in 28 days. Amazon MGM Studios: over $1.2 billion global box office in 2026.
  • Emmys move to Prime Video from 2027 through 2033, a deal worth about $15 million a year per an individual with knowledge (TheWrap, previously reported).
  • Amazon total net sales up 12% to $201.9 billion; profit $20.7 billion; shares fell over 5% after hours on an earnings miss.
