European Producers Say Netflix's Local Shows Come With Worse Terms Than Their Broadcasters
Netflix keeps the rights in every territory on its local originals, and no French scripted original besides Lupin has reached four seasons, producers told The Ankler.
In a report on what Peter Rice inherits as Netflix's new chief content officer, European producers said the "local for local" strategy limits their businesses. Robert Franke, former head of drama at ZDF Studios, said Netflix typically keeps the rights in every territory, while a show made for a local broadcaster can be sold abroad through distributors, potentially for more money. Pernel Media CEO Samuel Kissous said Netflix pays high budgets but orders few seasons. Netflix spent €308 million on French content, second only to France Télévisions. A source close to Netflix said local for local remains the strategy.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A Netflix order pays the budget but takes every territory, so a European producer gives up the international sales a broadcaster deal would allow, a trade that costs most on shows Netflix stops after one or two seasons.
The Facts
  • Context: Peter Rice replaced Bela Bajaria as Netflix chief content officer in October 2026. Netflix operates in 190 countries and produces local programming in 50; Enders Analysis says 40% of its viewers do not have English as their primary language.
  • Robert Franke (former head of drama, ZDF Studios; now runs Orange Chariot): Netflix "typically keeps the rights in every territory"; a show for a local broadcaster "can be sold abroad through international distributors, potentially for more money." Pitching English-language work to Netflix's German, Spanish or Italian teams is pointless, he said.
  • Samuel Kissous (CEO, Pernel Media): a Netflix commission is "a huge budget," but "high budgets but low volume and low return rates" make a sustainable production business hard. No French scripted original other than Lupin has reached four seasons.
  • France local content investment (Arcom): Netflix €308 million ($343 million); France Télévisions €470 million ($524 million).
  • Netflix laid off about 1,000 staff company-wide; about 2% of the U.K. office, including EMEA production VP Anna Mallett.
  • A source close to Netflix: the international strategy remains "local for local," its competitive differentiator, not scouting for global hits.
  • Netflix's Q3 letter said it will look for "new ways to bring more third-party content" after its TF1 deal in France.

Starz Now Owns Its Originals and Says the Payoff Is Just Beginning
Starz premiered Fightland, its first owned series since leaving Lionsgate, on July 31; a second season is in development and an owned Black Rodeo series is in production.
Starz reported third-quarter revenue of $322.4 million, up from $320.9 million, with streaming revenue of $226.6 million after an April price increase and linear revenue down to $95.8 million. Its net loss narrowed to $34.8 million from $52.6 million. CEO Jeffrey Hirsch said the company is "just beginning to unlock the financial upside of increased ownership." Since separating from Lionsgate in May 2025, Starz has developed IP in-house at a lower per-episode cost and drawn new series from Power and Outlander. Networks president Alison Hoffman said Starz also wants more tentpole acquisitions.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Starz now wants to own what it airs and to pay less per episode for it, so a producer selling Starz an original series is selling the copyright and the downstream revenue that comes with it.
The Facts
  • Q3 2026 (three months to September 30): revenue $322.4 million vs $320.9 million a year earlier; analyst consensus $319.5 million.
  • OTT revenue $226.6 million (higher renewal rates, April 2026 price increase); linear and other revenue $95.8 million (THR). Deadline reported OTT as $287 million; THR's figures sum to the total.
  • Net loss $34.8 million vs $52.6 million; adjusted OIBDA $44.2 million. Cash $86.8 million; total debt $687.5 million.
  • Jeffrey Hirsch, CEO: "we are just beginning to unlock the financial upside of increased ownership." 2026 outlook reiterated.
  • Owned originals: Fightland (premiered July 31; season 2 in development); untitled Black Rodeo series in production. Q4 slate adds the final season of P-Valley and two new Power series.
  • Michael (Antoine Fuqua) was the best-performing Pay 1 title in Starz history. S.W.A.T. Exiles, a spinoff of CBS's S.W.A.T., launched in September.
  • Alison Hoffman, Starz Networks president: Starz is "built to be bundled" (deals with Peacock, Crunchyroll, Amazon's five-service bundle) and is hunting more tentpole acquisitions.
  • Starz shares are up 85% year to date. Byron Allen sold his entire Starz stake the same day (Deadline headline).

Row K Has Stopped Distributing Films a Year After Buying Four at Toronto
Owner Media Capital Technologies froze all film distribution after Row K missed October payroll and rent, laid off four staff and fell behind on settlement payments, TheWrap reported.
Row K launched in August 2025, backed by Christopher Woodrow's Media Capital Technologies, and bought four films at the Toronto festival weeks later. Only two were released. Dead Man's Wire grossed under $4 million worldwide in January after Row K spent about $5 million to acquire it and $5 million to market it, an insider told TheWrap. The company gave up Maude Apatow's Poetic License, which Sony Pictures Classics picked up. President Megan Colligan left in the spring and Row K made no further acquisitions. MCT said it will refocus on its core business.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Row K bought four Toronto films on undisclosed backing and released two before freezing distribution, so a filmmaker selling to a new distributor is protected by a minimum guarantee paid at signing and rights that revert if no release comes.
The Facts
  • Media Capital Technologies (MCT) statement: it decided "to freeze all new activities related to film distribution and significantly reduce operating expenses, and refocus MCT exclusively on its core business."
  • Per TheWrap: Row K missed employee payroll and rent in October (and in August, per an insider), laid off four staff, missed health insurer payments, and is behind on settlement payments from confidential lawsuits settled this year.
  • Launch: Row K formed August 26, 2025, led by Christopher Woodrow and Raj Singh; Megan Colligan (former Imax and Paramount) named president. Funding described only as "significant."
  • TIFF 2025: four acquisitions; two released. Dead Man's Wire (January): under $4 million worldwide; about $5 million to acquire and $5 million to market, per an insider.
  • Poetic License (Maude Apatow's directorial debut) offloaded; Sony Pictures Classics acquired it.
  • Spring 2026: Colligan departed; Row K canceled its CinemaCon presentation and announced a pivot to a "more commercially focused slate," then made no acquisitions.
  • BANKEX is suing Woodrow, Castle Rock Digital LLC and MCT in New York State Supreme Court for at least $3 million.
  • Row K declined to comment beyond MCT's statement.
